For other National Risk Assessments visit: counteringfinancialcrime.im

This is the first standalone Terrorist Financing (TF) National Risk Assessment (NRA) and builds on the 2020 Money Laundering (ML)/TF NRA. The Isle of Man (IOM) carries several TF risks, taking into account its overall jurisdictional profile as an International Financial Centre (IFC), its geographic position and various materiality factors within its reporting sectors. As an IFC, the IOM is susceptible to a certain extent to the transit risk of TF, whereby funds may be channelled through the IOM financial system using the Banking sector and Trust and Corporate Service Provider (TCSP) sector by sophisticated actors servicing well-established terrorist organisations, including with state links.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 1. Ministerial Introduction - dfae1540658b773c
body:
Minister for Justice and Home Affairs Hon Jane Poole-Wilson MHK
Within our Island Plan , we lay the foundations to make the Isle of Man a more attractive and prosperous place to live and work, which in turn will sustain and grow productive businesses and services.
In support of our strategy, we prioritise a strong and diverse economy, of which a key pillar is our Isle of Man Financial Crime Strategy 2024-2026 .
We are committed to combatting all financial crime and upholding international standards. The Financial Action Task Force calls on jurisdictions to identify, assess and understand Terrorist Financing risks they face and to act to mitigate those risks effectively.
Whilst our Island is a comparatively safe place, we will make every effort to ensure terrorists cannot use our status as an International Finance Centre to finance their criminal activities. As an IFC, it is possible that we have some exposure to Terrorist Financing risk. This risk is constantly evolving, as criminal actors never stand still and, therefore, we constantly face new challenges. This report identifies areas where additional focus and action is required to further strengthen our controls.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 1. Ministerial Introduction - e2da3e4ef82d7d5c
body:
This is our first standalone Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment and is just one of the NRAs that the Island is currently undertaking. This extensive document will assist those in industry and the competent authorities and help demonstrate our ongoing compliance with international regulations. There will be outreach to industry in support of the publication of this document to help you understand and apply the key learnings.
The data available to support this NRA has improved considerably since the publication of our last Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing NRA in 2020. Thank you to everyone involved in collating, submitting, receiving and analysing the data. It helps to make our analysis more data-driven, in line with our strategy of ensuring that everyone works together and we have data to help evidence our effectiveness in our fight against Terrorist Financing.
As a responsible jurisdiction, our message is clear: we will not tolerate those who seek to commit crime either on or through our Island.
As we take an all-Island approach to tacking all types of financial crime, I wish to express my gratitude to everyone who has supported in the exercise to develop our first standalone Terrorist Financing NRA.
Why Write a Terrorist-Financing Specific NRA?

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary - 893f17be2f68063f
body:
Undertaking an NRA is a core requirement of the FATF, the international body responsible for setting and reviewing global standards for anti-money laundering and countering the financing of terrorism and the proliferation of weapons of mass destruction (AML/CFT/CPF). The FATF 40 Recommendations provide the international standards which all countries are expected to meet; it is IOM Government policy to adhere closely to these recommendations.
A country's understanding of risk is an essential foundation of its national AML/CFT/CPF regime and should be used to allocate resources efficiently across law enforcement, agencies and regulators, as well as by industry. Therefore, the IOM has produced this standalone TF NRA, to further enhance its understanding of the TF risks to which the jurisdiction may be exposed to as an IFC.
The overall objectives of this TF NRA are to:

- Build upon and enhance the understanding of the TF risks from the 2015 and 2020 Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing (ML/TF) NRAs

- Update on the TF actions recommended in the 2020 ML/TF NRA

- Provide the agencies, regulators and industry with a specific TF-focussed NRA.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary - ee24c5359c4dac8b
body:
The IOM carries several TF risks, taking into account its overall jurisdictional profile as an IFC, its geographic position and various materiality factors within its reporting sectors. As an IFC, the IOM is susceptible to a certain extent to the transit risk of TF, whereby funds may be channeled through the IOM financial system using the Banking sector and TCSPs sector by sophisticated actors servicing well-established terrorist organisations, including with state links. Temporary parking of such funds in investments products, including life insurance, may be a possible risk scenario, albeit with lower probability. In addition, TF may arise as a secondary activity to ML, where the proceeds of overseas criminality are laundered in the IOM and then sent cross-border to fund terrorism.
The IOM has considered the TF risks highlighted in the NRAs from both Jersey and Guernsey. Both jurisdictions are Crown Dependencies (CD) and also IFCs. Both Jersey and Guernsey highlighted the risk that exists of being used as a transit jurisdiction for the movement of funds linked to terrorist activity in another jurisdiction.
The scarcity of TF or terrorism information or the lack of criminal/intelligence cases, could potentially limit the identification and analysis of TF threats and vulnerabilities. A number of actions are recommended to mitigate this risk.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary - 45b8ef6301c09b61
body:
If the Island's controls against TF are not continually reviewed and improved, then there is a potential risk that the Island will be used by terrorist financiers.
This is the first standalone TF NRA and builds on the 2020 ML/TF NRA . It does not seek to unnecessarily duplicate the comprehensive work which supports the 2020 NRA and the recently published IOM Profile document , entitled "A Profile of the Isle of Man" and the reader is asked to refer to these documents.
The IOM Financial Crime Strategy 2024-2026 (National Financial Crime Strategy) clearly demonstrates publicly the very strong goal of tackling all forms of financial crime, including terrorist financing.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary, METHODOLOGY FOR THIS NRA - 7986a13d8a57f040
body:
The Island will continue to use World Bank (WB) methodology where available for its risk assessment work. WB methodology was used for the 2015 and 2020 ML/TF NRAs and has been used by many countries worldwide, including several other IFCs. In the WB methodology, the TF risk assessment tool treats TF risk as a product of two main components: threat and vulnerability . Figure 2-1 depicts the overall structure of the WB risk assessment tool . There are five steps, which this document follows in Chapters 6, 7 and 8:

- Step 1: TF Threat by Terrorist Organisations (results feed into Steps 2 and 3)

- Step 2: National TF Threat (results feed into Steps 3, 4 and 5) ● Step 3: Sectoral TF Risk (results feed into Steps 4 and 5)

- Step 4: National TF Vulnerability (results feed into Step 5)

- Step 5: National TF Risk (combination of all results).
Figure 2-1: Overall Structure of the World Bank Terrorist Financin Risk Assessment Tool g
Note 6: The consequences are integrated into those two components through weights, preconditions and network structure and are not assessed separately. This approach is adopted at both national and sectoral levels.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary, METHODOLOGY FOR THIS NRA - aaab7e024fc97c81
body:
Note 7: The TF Risk Assessment Tool consists of five Excel templates (which are called steps). Step 2: "National TF Threat" and Step 4: "National TF Vulnerability" are the core templates. The order of the steps is determined by the reliance of each step on the outputs from the foregoing step. Each subsequent step relies on the previous one. Step 5 combines all the results in two risk maps. The overall results are produced after all parts of the assessment have been completed and the results have been transferred to the interlinked modules, particularly to Step 5. The bold lines represent direct inputs into a subsequent step and dotted lines represent indirect inputs.
The risk assessment tool uses a logical model that relies on both qualitative and quantitative information. The scarcity of data on terrorism and TF within the IOM and globally is still a key impediment for the development of fully quantitative and data-based models. The WB tool adopts an approach that aims to make use of the best available qualitative and quantitative information to reach informed and reliable expert judgments on a series of factors that affect TF risks in the Island.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary, RISK ASSESSMENT STEPS, Step 1: TF Threat by Terrorist Organisations - 08763616e80f8ff7
headers: Step 1: TF Threat by Terrorist Organisations
body:
The Island is geographically situated between the United Kingdom (UK) and the Republic of Ireland and is away from globally recognised conflict zones and higher-risk jurisdictions. It is within the Common Travel Area (CTA) which protects free movement of people between the UK, the Republic of Ireland and the CDs .

The IOM has never experienced a domestic terrorist attack. The IOMC has a relevant intelligence gathering strategy. No terror groups or cells are believed to be active or present on the Island. There have been 4 offences between 2020/23, initially recorded when reported as terrorism offences, which were hoax calls to institutions such as schools. These were later assessed to be misuse of telecommunications rather than terrorism offences. There have been no terrorism offences and no terrorism financing offences within the scope of the time period of this NRA.

The IOM population profile is low risk for terrorism. Although there are significant numbers of people resident who were not born on the Island, very few originate from regions/countries with an elevated risk profile for terrorism. There have been no terrorism prosecutions or convictions.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary, RISK ASSESSMENT STEPS, Step 2: National TF Threat - bb215ae85b32e983
body:
Whilst there is a low threat from terrorism within the Island, there is an understanding that the Island may not be immune from the challenges faced in other countries and therefore consideration is given to the threats faced by our near neighbours, the UK and Republic of Ireland.
The UK's terror threat level is currently 'substantial'. In a recent speech the Director General of the UK Security Service stated, "The threat from terrorism, alongside ongoing efforts by autocratic states to harm the UK's security, presented the most complex threat environment we have ever seen".
Using WB methodology and with expert input from the Island's key agencies, Government and regulators, the national threat was assessed and categorised under four TF threat categories, see Figure 2-2. As would be anticipated for an IFC, the outgoing and transit TF threat came out highest.

body:
In addition to the national threat and national vulnerability, the threat and vulnerability were also considered in detail for 4 materially significant sectors to the Island. To support the analysis, industry bodies put forward representatives who assisted by attending workshops and providing their views and expert opinions.
A high-level assessment was undertaken for all the other sectors, apart from those where sectoral TF-related NRAs are planned.
Figure 2-3 presents the residual TF risk score to which each sector is exposed to, which derives from the TF threat to each sector and the residual vulnerability of the sector to TF. The 2020 ratings are taken from the 2020 ML/TF NRA and are the TF Risk ratings as presented in the NRA.
The methodology used to assess the TF risk scores for each sector in the 2020 ML/TF NRA differs from the TF-specific methodology used in this 2025 NRA. Any changes in the scoring may be attributed to several factors:

- A more in-depth analysis in 2025 has provided an enhanced understanding of a sector

- There has been substantive work across the sectors by the competent authorities and industry since 2020 to better understand TF threats and implement improved controls

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary, AWARENESS OF TF TYPOLOGIES - 77c8a3ea6aa3e877
body:
Generally, there is a lower understanding across both agencies and industry of TF and the forms it may take compared with ML. TF may be rarely, if ever, encountered whereas ML is more common. The lack of experience in the IOM in encountering TF, a lack of experience which is shared by many jurisdictions, may mean that any warning signs of TF and the threats of and vulnerabilities to TF might not be as readily identified as they would be for ML and suspicions may not be as readily engaged and reported as they would be for ML. The low number of TF Suspicious Activity Reports (SARs) may be because there has been very little TF or potential TF to date and/or it could be partly accounted for by the lack of experience in this area.

The jurisdiction's lack of experience in dealing with TF increases the need to raise the understanding (with the assistance of experience obtained from examples encountered in other jurisdictions) of the risks, threats and vulnerabilities of TF in all agencies and across all sectors. The typologies of TF, particularly those forms of TF at risk of being encountered in an IFC, need to continue to be collected from examples encountered in other jurisdictions and disseminated so that those in a position to report suspicions of TF have a better understanding of the forms in which it may be encountered.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary, TARGETED FINANCIAL SANCTIONS - dc475c76342a543b
body:
The Terrorism and Other Crime (Financial Restrictions) Act 2014 (TOCFRA) ensures that funds or other assets of a designated person sanctioned under a TF-related United Nations (UN) sanctions regime are frozen without delay and without prior notice. Under the UN sanctions regimes, there is an obligation to freeze all funds, financial assets or economic resources of designated persons.

No funds or other assets have been frozen in relation to designated persons or entities under the UN TF-related TFS regimes. However, IOM regulated entities have frozen assets linked to other sanctions regimes, including the UK's Russia regime which saw an unprecedented number of individuals and entities being designated following Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. This demonstrated that regulated entities understand their obligations regarding TFS.

Through examples of cooperation between agencies and actions taken in relation to other sanctions regimes, the Island can show that if there were an identified TF case, the Island would be capable of taking actions consistent with the requirements under respective UN sanctions regimes.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary, MONACO (MONEYVAL) SMALL STATES GUIDANCE ON IDENTIFYING, ASSESSING AND UNDERSTANDING THE RISK OF TF - 9f90d43ac8bae8c4
headers: MONACO (MONEYVAL) SMALL STATES GUIDANCE ON IDENTIFYING, ASSESSING AND UNDERSTANDING THE RISK OF TF
body:
Effective measures to address TF can only be put in place if the risks are understood. This can be a challenge for smaller financial centres, such as the IOM which is an IFC.
There are several challenges:

- An extremely limited number of cases to study and competent authorities who consequently may have little experience of TF activity. This challenge has been identified as a central one for small states, leading the IOM authorities to invest significant resources in addressing this issue: the creation of specialist teams (Proactive International Money Laundering Investigation Team (PIMLIT) within the IOMC and Financial Crime Unit (FCU) within Prosecution); additional resource within the FIU; additional resources within the Financial Services Authority (FSA) for both the AML/CFT and Enforcement divisions; additional resourcing for the Gambling Supervision Commission (GSC) AML/CFT team; in addition the Attorney General (AG) has issued internally the Prosecution Policy and Guidance on TF Prosecutions

- The difficulty in identifying potentially very small sums for which there is a terrorist purpose or to maintain small terrorist entities, versus the large sums required to maintain the largest terrorist entity

- The difficulty of assessing a risk that exists in another jurisdiction.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary, MONACO (MONEYVAL) SMALL STATES GUIDANCE ON IDENTIFYING, ASSESSING AND UNDERSTANDING THE RISK OF TF - 79ae5bc8be1dc4fc
headers: MONACO (MONEYVAL) SMALL STATES GUIDANCE ON IDENTIFYING, ASSESSING AND UNDERSTANDING THE RISK OF TF
body: Several smaller jurisdictions (including the IOM) met in Monaco in 2018 and 2024 to provide guidance on how they could identify, understand and assess these TF risks. This guidance has been used in this TF NRA in support of the WB methodology. Consideration of the cross-border exposure for a regulated entity as well as the Island are very important to the assessment of TF. In Chapter 7.2, this TF NRA considers a number of the risks identified in the Small States Guidance.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 2. Executive Summary, FINANCIAL FLOWS - e388c5b5e0324485
body:
The Island's banks supply the FSA with quarterly financial flow data , showing outflows and inflows by country as well as number of transactions. The funds coming into the IOM (and this equally applies to outflows) for SWIFT payments should pick up the original remitter for inflows and final beneficiary for outflows through the BIC code fields. The FSA has requested banks' internal audit functions to undertake additional audit work to re-verify this understanding. It should be noted that the UK figure includes Faster Payments , BACS and CHAPS payments.
This data was analysed to consider the top 10 countries for outflows and inflows as a percentage of the sum of the overall amounts for the four years, see Figure 2-7. The data highlights the strength of the connection with the UK, with 46.9% of the outflows and 51.1% of the inflows. However, the outflows data does not reveal whether the UK is the final destination or if the inflows ultimately originated in the UK.

A number of risks are identified throughout this TF NRA. As shown in Figure 2-12, the greater risks to the Island as an IFC are the Outgoing and Incoming Risks that are assessed as medium low and Transit Risks that is assessed as medium. Examples of some of these risks include:

- Shell companies which are inactive/dormant, but keep paying fees and then might be activated when required to receive/ transmit funds for a TF purpose

- Criminals setting up multiple companies with the IOM Companies Registry or UK Companies House for a TF purpose

- Complex layering for a TF purpose

- Terrorist property being processed through virtual assets

- Where a third country which the IOM has significant exposure to is placed under 'enhanced follow up' by the FATF. If it were then deemed to have strategic AML/CFT deficiencies, it would be placed on List A or Bi

- The immigration system being abused for TF

- The risks imported from other IFCs

- Displacement risk

- ML to fund TF

- Recruitment and retention of skilled professionals in industry and the agencies/regulators/Government to help prevent TF within the IOM.

Taking an average of the 4 TF Risk levels in Figure 2-11, the overall assessment score in 2025 of medium low aligns with previous TF assessments in NRAs, however it benefits from this more substantive document and is underpinned by a number of unpublished supporting workbooks. This risk assessment indicates that the risk of internal terrorist fund raising scores the lowest of the 4 categories and an overall medium risk of the IOM being used as a conduit (transit risk) for TF.
The assessment confirmed that there are areas where the IOM has adequate systems and controls in place to mitigate the risks of being used as a conduit for TF, as well as areas where additional focus and action is required to both test and strengthen existing controls and further develop understanding.
Significant progress has been made since the 2020 NRA in both understanding the TF risk and mitigating actions. The embedding of much better data from industry via the Regulators has allowed this NRA to have a deeper repository of data to review. Thanks must go to industry for supplying the FSA and GSC with the data on a quarterly/annual basis. Undoubtedly, these data requests will increase and broaden as the Island seeks to better understand the threats it faces. A number of additional data requests are recommended actions from this NRA.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 3. Introduction, 3.1 Terrorist Financing NRA, 3.1.1 Why Does the IOM Need a TF NRA? - 1a3624bf7e7d666a
headers: 3.1.1 Why Does the IOM Need a TF NRA?
body:
The FATF Recommendations require countries to identify, assess and understand the TF risks for the country, including designating an authority or mechanism to coordinate further actions in assessing TF risks and deploying resources, with the aim of ensuring that those risks are mitigated effectively. A country's understanding of risk is an essential foundation of its regulatory framework and should be used to allocate resources efficiently.
Many countries and jurisdictions produce a combined ML and TF NRA. The IOM produced a combined NRA in 2015 and another in 2020 . The International Monetary Fund (IMF) in its publication Countering the Financing of Terrorism: Good Practices to Enhance Effectiveness published May 2023 stated:
" The IMF's experience reveals that countries tend to combine terrorist financing risk assessments with money laundering risk assessments. This approach often leads to ineffective results because the risk indicators between terrorist financing and money laundering differ."

This approach often leads to ineffective results because the risk indicators between terrorist financing and money " . laundering differ The IOM has therefore produced this standalone TF NRA to enhance its understanding of the TF risks that the jurisdiction may be exposed to as an IFC.

headers: 3.1.2 Terrorist Financing Defined and How It Differs from Terrorism Risk
body:
As defined by the FATF , TF is the financing of terrorist acts and of terrorists and terrorist organisations.
The United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime (UNODC) defines TF as:

- " Terrorists and terrorist organisations usually need to rely on money to sustain themselves and to carry out terrorist acts. Terrorist financing encompasses the means and methods used by terrorist organisations to finance activities that pose a threat to national and international security. Money provides terrorist organisations with the capacity to carry out terrorist activities, which can be derived from a wide variety of sources. Money can come from both legitimate sources (i.e. profits from businesses and charitable organisations) and criminal sources (i.e. drug trade, weapon smuggling and kidnapping for ransom)."

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 3. Introduction, 3.1 Terrorist Financing NRA, 3.1.2 Terrorist Financing Defined and How It Differs from Terrorism Risk - 323dad2ff63986c4
headers: 3.1.2 Terrorist Financing Defined and How It Differs from Terrorism Risk
body:
In IOM legislation the Anti-Terrorism and Crime Act 2003 (ATCA) defines "terrorism" in Chapter 1. The Financing of Terrorism Fact Sheet published by the FSA provides a model to illustrate the stages which may form part of the financing of terrorism process, Figure 3-1. It should be noted that not all of these steps are required as part of the process. For example, raising funds will suffice for financing of terrorism to have occurred.
TF risk differs from the risk of terrorism. Terrorism risk refers to the likelihood and impact of terrorist attacks. TF risk is the involvement or exposure to the sources and methods of funding terrorist activities. A country may face a TF risk even if it is not a frequent target of terrorist attacks, as the property that facilitates terrorism may originate from or transit through different jurisdictions from the jurisdiction where the attacks take place. Figure 3-2 shows the paths of domestic and international flows of terrorist property within and between jurisdictions, adapted from The Negative Effects Of Money Laundering On Economic Development by Bartlett (May 2002) .

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 3. Introduction, 3.1 Terrorist Financing NRA, 3.1.3 Challenges in Understanding TF Risk - bd10f825c7bc6bf3
body:
In the FATF report, Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment Guidance (July 2019) , it emphasises some of the challenges jurisdictions face in understanding TF risk, including:

- the difficulty of detecting low-value and diverse TF activities that use small amounts of funds or assets and exploit a wide range of sectors

- the scarcity of TF or terrorism information and expertise domestically or the lack of criminal/intelligence cases, that limit the identification and analysis of TF threats and vulnerabilities

- the tendency to overlook or conflate TF risk with terrorism risk in NRAs, with insufficient attention paid to the specific threats posed by terrorist financiers and sympathisers

- the need for a customised TF risk assessment approach that reflects the unique threat profile, national context and Countering Terrorism (CT)/CFT strategies of each jurisdiction which draws upon relevant guidance and country examples.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 3. Introduction, 3.1 Terrorist Financing NRA, 3.1.4 Data Used - abe78f7b50f30f80
body:
Since the completion of the last ML/TF NRA in 2020, the data available across the jurisdiction has continued to improve. In 2023, the FSA/GSC launched STRIX AML, which enables the FSA/GSC to receive, risk assess and analyse data from the regulated sector. The system assists the FSA/GSC in analysing the data submitted by industry in an efficient manner. The data is then used to build entity, sectoral and NRAs and drive the supervisory engagement model for the FSA/GSC. It also allows for cross-sectoral comparisons to be made.

This NRA uses data from 2020 (the publication of the last ML/ TF NRA) up to 2023. It also includes a limited amount of 2024 data where available and relevant. Data has been compiled by a number of the agencies, government departments and regulators in the jurisdiction. Where sensitive data has been used, it has been aggregated to allow inclusion in this report, displayed as percentages rather than actuals or removed from the final published version of this report.

As is the case for many countries and jurisdictions, there are very limited cases to reference and so typologies and cases from other jurisdictions' open-source information are referenced. Where there are significant gaps in the data, then actions are recommended to establish new frameworks for data collection and that these be included in the National Action Plan.

This is the first standalone TF NRA, therefore it builds on the 2020 ML/TF NRA. It does not seek to unnecessarily duplicate the comprehensive work which supports the initial NRAs and the recently published IOM Profile document, entitled "A Profile of the Isle of Man" and the reader is asked to refer to these documents.

The National Financial Crime Strategy, which incorporates the mission, aims, strategic objectives and actions, clearly demonstrates publicly the very strong goal of tackling all forms of financial crime, including terrorist financing. In Appendix 4 of The National Financial Crime Strategy document, a timeline is provided for the key activities in the development and maintenance of the Island's AML/CFT/CPF regime in line with international standards.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 3. Introduction, 3.3 Methodology - 489e288bb8a9fd03
body:
The National Financial Crime Strategy states in strategic objective two: "Use a risk-based approach to identify risk, coordinate appropriate actions and apply resources to ensure identified risk is addressed and mitigated". The AML/CFT Policy Office team within the Government's Cabinet Office co-ordinates the NRA work. It will continue to use WB methodology where available for its risk assessment work. WB methodology was used for the 2015 and 2020 ML/TF NRAs. It has been used to provide consistency with previously published NRAs.
In the WB methodology, the TF risk assessment tool treats TF risk as a product of two main components: threat and vulnerability. The consequences are integrated into those two components through weights, preconditions and network structure and are not assessed separately. This approach is adopted at both national and sectoral levels for the IOM. TF threat primarily considers activities or persons with the potential to cause harm by raising, moving, storing or using funds or other assets for terrorist purposes, while TF vulnerabilities consider the design of the frameworks to mitigate risk and any weaknesses or gaps in the defence against TF that could be exploited by the threat or that may support or facilitate its activities.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 3. Introduction, 3.3 Methodology - d61df5752d2a6796
body:
The WB methodology is not a statistical model approach as there is not enough data in many jurisdictions, including the IOM. The Island's experts have decided on the ratings using the qualitative and quantitative data together and making an expert judgement which is supported by evidence as much as possible. WB methodology uses both qualitative and quantitative information.
The scarcity of data on terrorism and TF globally is still a key impediment for the development of fully quantitative and databased models. However, the analysis has been enhanced by the varied sources of data available, especially from the AML/CFT returns and financial flow data, which have allowed the Island to better understand the immediate, emerging and ongoing threats of TF via data.
In the WB TF risk assessment tool there are five steps, which this document follows in Chapters 6, 7 and 8:

- Step 1: TF Threat by Terrorist Organisations (results feed into Steps 2 and 3)

- Step 2: National TF Threat (results feed into Steps 3, 4 and 5)

- Step 3: Sectoral TF Risk (results feed into Steps 4 and 5)

- Step 4: National TF Vulnerability (results feed into Step 5)

- Step 5: National TF Risk (combination of all results).
Each step is supported by WB Excel sheets and steps 2, 3 and 4 are underpinned by extensive workbooks which have not been published, that provide the summary narrative for this document.

body:
Appendices 2 and 3 in the 2020 ML/TF NRA summarised the legal and regulatory framework as well as the legislation, as does the recently published IOM Profile document, entitled "A Profile of the Isle of Man".

The fourth and most recent National Financial Crime Strategy, published in November 2023, established the mission, aims and strategic objectives for the continued success of the IOM as an IFC. The aims are:

- Public sector and industry work together to achieve a common goal of meeting international standards

- Actions are informed and driven by best practice and standards, both domestic and internationally

- The Island is an active participant in the global fight against financial crime

- All stakeholders have the resources they need to effectively identify and respond to ML/TF/PF threats.

The National Financial Crime Strategy clearly documents the IOM's position in supporting international efforts in the fight against all forms of TF. Figure 4-1 shows the relation between the overall Island Plan and the National Financial Crime Strategy. The National Action Plan, once published, will outline the actions being taken by which competent authority. The National Risk Appetite, which is scheduled to be drafted within the next 12 months and a number of NRAs, of which this TF NRA is one core part.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 4. Legal, Supervisory & Law Enforcement Framework, 4.2 Framework - bd789809cca4329d
body:
The IOM's CFT framework includes a robust suite of legislation and other enforcement tools. It includes a dissuasive array of sanctions. This framework:

- a) is established to minimise the abuse of the international financial system by actors wishing to finance terrorism

- b) is based on the FATF Recommendations and is continually updated in line with the FATF changes

- c) implements the requirements of the international conventions extended to the IOM, including the United Nations Terrorist Financing Convention (International Convention for the Suppression of the Financing of Terrorism 1999).

The Island achieved a high level of compliance with the FATF 40 Recommendations at the time of the last MONEYVAL assessment, with 39 out of the 40 being scored compliant or largely compliant. The two key pieces of legislation relating to TF in IOM legislation are:

- ATCA 2003

- TOCFRA 2014 .

headers: 5. Update on TF Actions from 2020 ML/TF NRA
body:
The 2020 IOM ML/TF NRA made 5 recommendations at the end of Chapter 5, Main Threats - Terrorist Financing Threats.
1. The full analysis and understanding of inflows and outflows of funds to higher-risk jurisdictions
- Data on the monetary value and volume of inflows and outflows for all 11 banks including origin and destination of funds, which is now collected and analysed quarterly by the FSA and shared with the FIU
- The aggregated results identify where financial flows are received from and are sent to; this includes higher-risk jurisdictions. The data is also used by the FIU to support ongoing strategic analysis projects
- The FSA Sector reports which are published include details of year-on-year payment flows in and out and the highest-risk countries
- The data is used in this and other NRAs
- In Chapter 7.2.2 it is recommended that Class 8 Money Transmission Services also provide financial flow data to the FSA.
2. Using the information and data collated from the regulatory annual returns to further inform supervisory work and preventive measures
- In 2016 - 17 the FSA worked with Financial Institutions (FIs) to devise a dedicated AML/CFT return. The first cross-sectoral return was completed by all FIs and a number of DNFBPs in 2017 on a best endeavours basis. The annual return was revised following feedback and further returns from all FIs and DNFBPs submitted in 2018 (for 2017 data) and 2019 (for 2018 data)

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.1 Step 1: Threat by Terrorist Organisation, 6.1.1 Introduction - e083160a34f673d9
body:
The TF threat increases if there are active terrorist organisations in a jurisdiction. Step 1 of the WB methodology considers this threat. The threat posed, is assessed by considering all active terrorist organisations or types (such as lone wolf) and reviewing per organisation:

- TF threat

- Diagnostic of TF methods:

- What are the funding needs and the possible sources of funding

- Assets - movement and use of funds

- Which channels are used for moving funds.

By understanding the organisations, there is a greater understanding of the TF threat and this informs the overall TF threat assessment in Step 2. As documented in the FATF Terrorist Financing Report, February 2008 :

"The first step in identifying and forestalling the flow of funds to terrorists is to understand the funding requirements of modern terrorist groups. The costs associated not only with conducting terrorist attacks but also with developing and maintaining a terrorist organisation and its ideology are significant. Funds are required to promote a militant ideology, pay operatives and their families, arrange for travel, train new members, forge documents, pay bribes, acquire weapons and stage attacks. Often, a variety of higher-cost services, including propaganda and ostensibly legitimate social or charitable activities are needed to provide a veil of legitimacy for organisations that promote their objectives through terrorism."

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.1 Step 1: Threat by Terrorist Organisation, 6.1.2 Isle of Man: Domestic Terrorist Threat - 7df160b6f0bcdf51
headers: 6.1.2 Isle of Man: Domestic Terrorist Threat
body:
The IOM has never experienced a terrorist attack. The IOMC has a relevant intelligence gathering strategy. No terror groups or cells are believed to be active or present on the Island. The IOM population profile is low-risk for terrorism. Although there are significant numbers of people resident who were not born on the Island, very few originate from regions/countries with an elevated risk profile for terror. There have been no terrorism prosecutions or convictions.
Given its small island population of 84,069 , this is similar to the finding in the TF NRA for a number of other smaller jurisdictions. However, as an IFC, this does not necessarily result in no TF risk. Consequently, the Island contributed to the Monaco
MONEYVAL workshop which produced guidance for assessing TF risk for IFCs with low domestic terrorism risk, detailed within the FATF Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment Guidance (2019). See Chapter 7.2 of this NRA.
There have been 4 offences between 2020 - 2023 initially recorded when reported as terrorism offences, which were hoax calls to institutions such as schools. These were later assessed to be misuse of telecommunications rather than terrorism offences and there have been no prosecutions for any terrorism offence. The IOM Department of Home Affairs publishes a list of proscribed organisations , which are the same as those listed in Schedule 2 of the UK Terrorism Act 2000 . "Proscribed organisations" are defined in the UK Act.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.1 Step 1: Threat by Terrorist Organisation, 6.1.3 UK: Domestic Terrorist Threat - 50d31fe09034db16
body:
"The UK national threat level incorporates the threat from far-right terrorism and left-wing, anarchist and single-issue terrorism in addition to Islamist terrorism and Northern Ireland-related terrorism in mainland Great Britain. Far-right terrorism encompasses ideologies adopted that can commonly be subdivided into cultural nationalism, white nationalism and white supremacism. Although Islamist terrorism remains the greatest threat in the UK, far-right terrorism has evolved in recent years and is of growing concern both within the UK and across Europe. Left-wing, anarchist and single-issue terrorism covers a broad spread of threat strands that sit outside of far-right terrorism: political left, anarchist and single issue. For example, anti-state, animal rights abuses, environmental abuses and anti-democracy. Most terrorist attacks and plots in the UK continue to be planned by British residents… continuing to see a trend towards lone actor, low sophistication attacks, which are inherently harder to detect."
According to the published UK Home Office figures, there were 159 arrests for terrorism-related activity in the UK for the year ending 30 June 2023. As at 30 June 2023, there were 234 persons in custody for terrorism-connected offences in Great Britain. Of those in custody, the majority (65%) were categorised as holding Islamist-Extremist views; a further 27% were categorised as holding Extreme Right-Wing ideologies and 8% were categorised as holding 'Other' ideologies.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.1 Step 1: Threat by Terrorist Organisation, 6.1.3 UK: Domestic Terrorist Threat - d59acca6f009f174
body:
In a recent speech the Director General of the UK Security Service stated: "The threat from terrorism, alongside ongoing efforts by autocratic states to harm the UK's security, presented the most complex threat environment we have ever seen".
RUSI in their paper "The Silent Threat, The Impact of Fraud on UK National Security" January 2021 highlights that as terrorism moves from large organisations such as Al-Qa'ida to small cells and lone actors, the funding from fraudulent activities has become more prevalent.
These UK threats have been considered for the IOM, as per WB methodology. Whilst the UK and IOM are very closely linked, the threat from UK domestic terrorists using the IOM financial system is considered to be very low, given the physical separation and onboarding controls. There are a number of Irish and Northern Irish IOM residents; however, the Island has no history of sectarian tension. There are no active political groups linked to Irish Republicanism. No intelligence exists to suggest Republican Paramilitary Groups have a presence or any substantial body of sympathisers. There is no indication of fund raising or money laundering linked to such groups.

body: It should be noted that there is a close working relationship between the IOM and the UK. As documented in CONTEST: The United Kingdom's Strategy for Countering Terrorism (2023) , the UK has responsibility to the Crown Dependencies (which includes the IOM) stemming from international law and the constitutional relationship. The UK would support any locally led response if an incident occurred. The IOMC primarily engages with the UK Counter Terrorism network through the 'Pursue' and 'Prevent' strands. If there were a situation of terrorism with a primarily external nexus (UK-based/affecting the UK/ international), the UK National Crime Agency or the British Security Services would be the lead agency for identification and investigation and the IOM agencies would support.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.1 Step 1: Threat by Terrorist Organisation, 6.1.4 Ireland: Domestic Terrorist Threat - 469edece88af592d
body:
The Global Terrorism Index (2024) scores Ireland as 0.03 and an overall rank of 88. This is the lowest (most favourable) score for countries that are rated. The Fragile States Index (2023) rates Ireland as 'Very Sustainable' with a score of 19.5, one of the most favourable scores globally.

The Ireland ML/TF NRA 2019 explains that:

"Republican Paramilitary Groups (sometimes referred to as 'dissident groups') represent the main terrorist threat to the security of the State. While the Good Friday Agreement has delivered a stable peace process that commands overwhelming cross-community support, certain groups in both communities, with very limited levels of support, remain intent on disrupting the progress which has been achieved. It is important to understand that these groups operate on a 'whole of island' basis, with activities occurring on both sides of the border. While logistical support, planning and financing may occur in both jurisdictions, these groups do not generally have as an objective the carrying out of acts of terrorism in this State. For that reason it is generally assessed that an attack in Ireland from this source is unlikely."

The threats from Ireland have been considered for the IOM, as per WB methodology. Europol's Terrorism Situation and Trend Report (2023) recorded 19 arrests in Ireland in 2022. This highlights that whilst the IOM is not currently directly affected, neighbouring countries may be impacted.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.1 Step 1: Threat by Terrorist Organisation, 6.1.4 Ireland: Domestic Terrorist Threat, LONE ACTORS - b77d4fe795e6ecc9
body:
The Europol Terrorism Situation and Trend Report looks at the outlook on potential developments in terrorism and violent extremism in the European Union (EU). Figure 6-2 summarises the report's comments on lone actors. The threats from lone actors have been considered for the IOM, as per WB methodology.

Figure 6-2: Lone Actors

Acting alone but not unconnected, Lone Actors are expected by Europol to continue to perpetrate most of the terrorist attacks in the EU. The range of ideas, messages and grievances that can trigger radicalisation is expected to become even broader in the background of social polarisation and recurrent economic crises. Against such backdrop and strongly enabled by the almost unconstrained access to online extremist and terrorist content, more vulnerable individuals without prior and direct affiliation to terrorism or violent extremism can be exposed to radical content and ideas.

As a countermeasure to deflect law enforcement investigations, terrorist networks may target vulnerable individuals and influence/manipulate them to commit terrorist acts as lone actors, seemingly alone, but in reality serving the objectives of the larger networks.

Step 2 considers the national threat of TF. As per earlier Figure 3-1, it assesses the aspects of raising, moving, storing and using of funds to finance terrorism, terrorist organisations and people. Figure 6-3 details WB methodology for Step 2.
The assessment of the national TF threat considered by the experts on Island, covered:

1. Active terrorist threat in the jurisdiction, including: current level of alert system (if any); casualties; terrorist acts; ancillary activities; overall impact of terrorism

2. Terrorist organisations which includes the input from Step 1 (Chapter 6.1), threat by terrorist organisations

3. Sympathisers, including: level of investigations-prosecutionsconvictions; SARs; travel to active zones; outgoing remittances to geographical locations that have an active terrorist threat; Islanders having close relationships to active zones

4. Threat from neighbouring jurisdictions, including: neighbours' threat level (Chapters 6.1.3 and 6.1.4); fatalities in neighbouring countries; terrorist acts; funding needs associated with the active terrorist threat of neighbouring jurisdictions

5. Finance and Trade Hub, which captures elements applicable to the IOM as an IFC, supported by Chapter 7.2, Monaco (MONEYVAL) Small States guidance

6. Strategic goods and services including: providing strategic goods, services or financial aid to affected areas.
The assessment then produced outputs (0-1.0) in four categories, as per Figure 6-4.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.2 Step 2: National TF Threat, 6.2.2 TF Threat Arising From Active Terrorist Threat - 880751b19107225c
headers: 6.2.2 TF Threat Arising From Active Terrorist Threat
body:
The IOMC has a MOU in place with UK LEAs which provides intelligence updates around relevant threats and risks relating to terrorism. The working collaboration also provides a basis for mutual support where necessary and development and learning to IOM intelligence and investigation staff.
The UK terrorism strategy is built around the four 'P's approach which relates to;

- Pursue - stopping terrorist attacks

- Prevent - stopping people becoming terrorists or supporting violent extremism

- Protect - strengthening our protection against terrorist attack

- Prepare - mitigating the impact of attacks.
The IOMC has embraced the principles of this working strategy within local domestic examples where potential terrorist offending has been identified. These principles were employed and active working strategies developed relating to bespoke matters of interest to protect the IOM. In particular, where there has been any evidence relating to potential radicalisation, the IOMC have assessed and put mitigation measures in place to prevent and protect with any cases to date resulting in no further action in relation to any terrorist concerns.
Where appropriate the IOMC has engaged with other stakeholders across the Island, such as prison and probation services, mental health services, education and other agencies where the principles and mitigation action in line with the Prevent strategy has been taken forward or advice offered.

body:
There is no intelligence in the IOM to suggest links with so-called Foreign Terrorist Fighters (FTF) and their funding. However, it is well documented that the risk posed by FTFs does exist throughout the world and therefore as an IFC it is important that there is an awareness of the threat. The United Nations Security Council Counter-Terrorism Committee Executive Directive issued a report titled Evolving Trends in the Financing of Foreign Terrorist Fighters' Activity: 2014-2024 , published in November 2024. The report summarises how financial flows related to FTF travel and activities have evolved over the ten-year period. It highlights that there are at least 35,000 - 45,000 FTF associated individuals remain in camps and prisons. It concludes on evolving trends and how these will shape the landscape of FTF financing:
- "The decentralization of terrorist groups is likely to lead to a corresponding decentralization in their financing methods, including in relation to any associated FTFs
- Armed conflict contexts in which FTFs operate also raise challenges for impartial humanitarian action where measures to counter the financing of terrorism may result in negative unintended consequences on the provision of vital humanitarian aid Technological advancements will continue to play an important role in the evolution of FTF financing, with an anticipated further increase and sophistication in exploitation of new and emerging financial technologies"

- Technological advancements will continue to play an important role in the evolution of FTF financing, with an anticipated further increase and sophistication in exploitation of new and emerging financial technologies as they continue to spread across jurisdictions
- The convergence between terrorist financing and transnational organized crime networks is likely to continue, particularly for financing and FTF-associated travel facilitation purposes
- The increased convergence in the mixed use of old and new ways to raise and move funds (e.g., online fundraising in virtual assets and with further use of hawala-like systems or cash couriers to move collected funds) essentially combines the challenges and complexities related to each method - from detecting physical cross-border transportation of cash to tracing intricate virtual transactions."

This typology is described in the UK Neighbourhood Watch website : Signs of terrorist activity.
Like other criminals, terrorists need to plan. They need to prepare, to buy and store materials and find ways to fund their activities. Much of this is done in view of the public. It can be hard to distinguish between terrorist activity and ordinary activity or behaviour, but the police would prefer that you report anything that you find suspicious, even if you are not sure.
For example: Your neighbour travels a lot but is vague about where they are going and why they are visiting that country.
As detailed in Chapter 6.1, the key neighbouring jurisdictions are the UK and Republic of Ireland. Both have sophisticated anti-terror agencies and their NRAs give a good understanding of the risks they face and hence help the IOM consider the risks of any proximate TF threat. The UK ML/TF NRA 2020 states: "Most terrorist attacks and plots in the UK continue to be planned by British residents continuing to see a trend towards lone actor, low sophistication attacks, which are inherently harder to detect." The UK NRA explains the close economic ties between the UK and the Crown Dependencies and the significant economic benefits, although it does state that criminals seek to exploit this relationship. The Irish ML/TF NRA 2019 makes no explicit reference to the Island.
The United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism in an article entitled Cybersecurity and New Technologies warns about the growing concern of terrorists misusing information and the internet and new technologies in particular. They are used to 'commit, incite, recruit, fund or plan acts of terrorism'. In 2024 the United Nations Interregional Crime and Justice Research Institute published a report titled Beneath the Surface: Terrorist and Violent Extremist Use of the Dark Web and Cybercrime as a Service for Cyber-Attacks (June 2024) . chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.2 Step 2: National TF Threat, 6.2.6 TF Threat Arising From Finance and Trade Hub - 6c99f371505266a0
headers: 6.2.6 TF Threat Arising From Finance and Trade Hub
body:
Financial and trade hubs, particularly those with international and regional significance, often present an appealing environment for TF activities. This remains true even in areas with minimal or no active terrorist threats or where few terrorist organisations, individuals or groups operate. These hubs potentially offer facilities that can be exploited for TF purposes, with the sheer scale of global financial transactions making it challenging to identify suspicious activities. Additionally, trade hubs may attract financing flows related to goods such as military or strategic items, contraband or assets acquired by terrorist organisations, including resources like oil or antiquities. The high volume of goods passing through these hubs generally complicates efforts to enforce laws and detect illicit operations. Such vulnerabilities can be especially significant for jurisdictions, neighbouring areas or major trading partners facing an active terrorist threat.
The Island is not a transhipment hub or a major trading hub (most trade is with the UK), however it is an IFC and therefore rated as medium. The threat is deemed to be constant and not changing significantly at present.

WB methodology seeks to assess the risk of sectors in the jurisdiction, to help fully understand the national TF risk. Not only may the features of a sector lend themselves to being exploited by terrorist financiers, but weaknesses in the CFT measures in different sectors may also cause TF vulnerability. However, due to the different nature of terrorist financing crimes, not all sectors require an in-depth TF risk assessment. Each jurisdiction must first decide which sectors should be subjected to an in-depth risk assessment and for which others a brief risk assessment would be sufficient.
FATF Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment Guidance 2019 states:

- " An assessment of TF risk will require a consideration of both cross-border risks and TF risks posed to specific sectors. The extent to which countries will need to assess the TF risks posed to specific sectors will depend to some extent on the materiality, TF awareness and geographic reach of certain sectors."
For the Island the following sectors have been reviewed using the WB Sector methodology:

- Banks

- TCSPs

- Life Insurance

- Online Gaming

- In addition, the NPO TF NRA will be published shortly after the publication of this NRA.

body:
The FSA has published its Supervisory Methodology Framework in January 2025. This details how the FSA approaches the supervision of Groups. When conducting our supervisory activities we also take into account where there is more than one firm within the same corporate group and how integrated the systems, business models, controls and governance is for firms within those groups.

The FSA is an active participant in supervisory colleges, which are viewed by the FSA as an important component of their supervisory activities. They help the FSA to share information with other regulators about financial services groups with a presence on the Island (typically high and medium impact firms, most notably in respect of banks and certain insurers), improve the FSA's understanding of risk and learn about market and regulatory developments. The FSA may organise and chair a supervisory college, where they are the home supervisor or as other circumstances may apply (for example for larger fiduciary groups or for insurance groups if the FSA are the "group supervisor") or the FSA may be invited, as a host supervisor, to attend a college arranged by an overseas home regulatory supervisor.

body:
Throughout this document, consideration is given to the exposure that regulated entities and their customers may have to jurisdictions that are considered likely to be subjected to a greater level of threat from terrorism and TF. The Island has categorised countries by the risk they pose :

- 'List A' contains those jurisdictions which the FATF has made a call on its members and other jurisdictions to apply countermeasures to protect the international financial system from the on-going and substantial risks of ML/TF emanating from the jurisdiction. List A currently comprises 3 jurisdictions

- 'List B' contains those jurisdictions with strategic AML/CFT deficiencies or which may pose a higher-risk of ML/TF. List B is made up of two lists:

- List Bi - consists of countries that FATF has identified as having strategic AML/CFT deficiencies for which they have developed an action plan with the FATF. It also identifies a number of jurisdictions as not having made sufficient progress on their action plans agreed with the FATF

- List Bii - specifies additional jurisdictions that have also been identified as those that may pose a higher-risk of ML or TF by the IOM Government. The list is prepared, in accordance with an established methodology, using data gathered from various commercial intelligence sources that cover ML, TF, crime, transparency and bribery/corruption risk.

Further, South Africa is just one country component of a wider exposure to African-based clients in respect of not only the South African banks that operate from the Island, but some other banks that had built previous relationships on that continent. Included within these customer numbers are a very small number of overseas-based charities (not registered on the IOM Charities Register) who hold monies with IOM banks. Whilst the majority are UK registered charities, a small number are African-registered charities. The banks also support the IOM charitable sector with Banking facilities, with 0.6% being rated as higher-risk.
The cash activity in the Banking sector will be via the domestic branches. CFT Control Factors for Banking Rating 1 Comprehensiveness of CFT Legal/Regulatory Framework
0.8 Very High
There are comprehensive laws and regulations regarding CFT. In the IOM the two key pieces of legislation relating to TF are ATCA and TOCFRA.
The Banking sector is supervised by the FSA. The FSA issue and maintain the AML/CFT Handbook.
The Isle of Man's AML/CFT framework of legislation and guidance is drafted to meet the FATF AML/CFT standards. AML/CFT legislation as defined by the Code means:

- Section 7 to 11 and 14 of ATCA

- Part 3 of the Proceeds of Crime Act 2008 (POCA)

- Parts 2 to 4 of TOCFRA

- financial sanctions which have effect on the Island

- the Code.
The AML/CFT Handbook provides extensive guidance across a range of matters that are key to the Banking sector.
The FIU also issues guidance to banks on completing SARs, as well as providing feedback on the quality of SARs.
2 Effectiveness of Supervision/Oversight Activities 0.8 Very High
The FSA has published its Countering Financial Crime Strategic Approach document , which sets out the mission and vision taking direction from the FSA's Strategic Plan for 2024 - 27 .
The Financial Services Act 2008 (FSA08) prescribes the mandate and powers to the FSA. The FSA inspections methodology (October 2021) is also published . The FSA's supervisory framework was published in May 2023 . The document details where the policies and procedures fit into the control considerations.

The FSA has been receiving AML/CFT annual returns and financial flow data from banks for the last 7 years which informs the risk-based approach to Supervision as well as informing sector reports which are published on the FSA's website. The use of technology (STRIX AML) has further streamlined this process and allows for the efficient analysis of risk producing a risk heat map of both sectors and individual entities.
Through the publication of sector reports and the analysis of the AML/CFT returns (including financial flows) the staff within the FSA have a good understanding of the risks within the banking sector and are confident in determining where to focus resources when devising the Engagement Plan.
Figure 6-16: Number of AML/CFT Inspections & Thematic Questionnaires of Banks by the FSA Since Q1 2020
As stated in the FSA AML/CFT Supervisory Priorities 2025/27 document : "A key part of our approach to assessing risk at firm and sector level is through data collection and automation, as well as intelligence and other information, including onsite and desk-based fieldwork."
In addition to AML/CFT annual returns, thematic reviews and supervisory inspections covering AML/ CFT, the FSA holds discussions with the banks' internal audit and compliance teams and has meetings/dialogue with the IOM Banking Association on matters where required.

3 Availability and Enforcement of Administrative Sanctions 0.8 Very High The FSA seek to:

- Intervene at an early justified stage in issues to help prevent unacceptable risks crystallising

- Understand, collaborate and follow a reasonable path of remediation to achieve the right outcomes

A full suite of regulatory measures is available and applicable including both criminal and civil penalties, including against individuals. Administrative sanctions include directions, conditions, suspension and revocation.

The FSA's Licensing Policy for Regulated Activities under the FSA08 sets out the criteria that applicants must satisfy to be successful in securing and retaining a financial services licence. The FSA will not issue a licence unless it is satisfied that the licence applicant, including the persons associated with it, is a fit and proper person to undertake the regulated activity. The fit and proper test is both an initial test at the time of granting a licence and a continuing test in relation to the conduct of regulated activities. The test takes into account integrity, financial standing and competence.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.2 Banking Sector, 6.3.2.4 Summary for Banking sector, BANKING SECTOR OVERVIEW - f2c65bf81a575d1e
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The Island's banking sector is well-established, fully regulated and supervised by the FSA, with robust CFT supervision measures in place. Most banks operate as branches or subsidiaries of larger banking groups and are subject to broader group-wide consolidated supervision, requiring compliance with both local and group-wide CFT regulations. The quality of controls was deemed to be medium.
These banks serve a diverse range of clients, including local and international personal customers, corporate entities and individuals managing funds on behalf of others (e.g. wealth management services).
Their customer base spans various nationalities and locations and they offer an extensive range of products and services. Approximately 96% of transactions are cross-border. The largest trading partner for the IOM is the UK, which accounts for 46.9% of outward payments and 51.1% of inward payments over the most recent 4-year period.
It is globally recognised that bank products do provide some suitability for TF, as they enable person-to-person transfers, via digital or mobile banking. However, over recent years the banks have generally sought to de-risk the customer base, partly as a result of the cost of retaining higher-risk business (in a lower interest rate environment) and the cost via regulatory penalties and remediation when obligations are not met. Consequently, the inherent TF risk was assessed as medium.
Overall, the residual TF risk the banking sector is exposed to is medium.

It is possible that an individual terrorist or a terrorist organisation may seek to disguise themselves as and appear to operate like a legitimate individual or business to use an IFC and the services offered by TCSP for the purposes of TF. Terrorist financiers may be attracted to use the IOM for the cover of legitimacy that an IOM or British company and/or trust, particularly when used as part of a multi-jurisdictional structure, might provide. The stacking of legal persons and/or legal arrangements across jurisdictions may be used to launder money and/or to finance terrorism. There is always the risk that a TCSP might be used to finance terrorism either wittingly or (and this may be more likely) unwittingly, especially if the TCSP has weak controls and a poor AML/CFT framework.
As an IFC, the client base of the TCSPs is global and this imports country risk.

The cash activity in the TCSP sector is negligible. In the AML/CFT annual returns for 2023, TCSP firms stated :

- Incoming cash: 6.3% of firms accept cash by exception and 93.8% never accept cash

- Outgoing cash: 3.1% of firms send cash by exception, 94.8% never send cash and 2.1% will send occasionally.
Where TCSPs are signatories to the accounts of their clients, they consider a payment before it is made, rather than review retrospectively, which helps to mitigate the risk.
The size of the TCSP potentially has an impact on the inherent vulnerabilities, see Figure 6-22 which shows what percentage of the IOM's TCSP sector by size of TCSPs. (Source IOM Government):

- Smaller TCSPs may not have the economies of scale to invest in systems which larger firms have

- Larger TCSPs may be part of wider groups and may be able to call upon specialist resources which smaller TCSPs may not

- Ownership of the TCSP may affect the culture and risk appetite.
Several TCSPs support Online Gambling firms, so Chapter 6.3.5 should also be considered by those TCSPs when they update their BRA.
Figure 6-22: TCSP Size
Source: IOM Government
From the annual AML/CFT returns the sector advised that in 2023 it provided services to:

- 18,001 companies

- 11,673 trusts.

headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
6.3.3.2 Inherent Vulnerability Factors for TCSP Sector to TF
body:
There is inherent vulnerability of the TCSP sector potentially being misused for TF (just as for ML):

- The ability to conceal/disguise the identity of the individual(s) who control the company or trust and its purpose

- The use of shell companies which may for long periods be inactive/dormant, but still administered by the TCSP whose fees continue to be paid. Such companies may acquire a spurious legitimacy from their longevity but are ready to be activated if required to receive/transmit funds for TF

- Criminals setting up multiple companies with the IOM Companies Registry or UK Companies House, one or more of which may be used for the purposes of TF. The UK Companies House Strategic Intelligence Assessment published in October 2024, details where mass incorporations have been evidenced

- Complex layering - see Chapter 7.2.4

- Property being processed through virtual assets

- The splitting of control/management of the trust or corporate structure across several stacked jurisdictions

- The use of different Virtual Asset Exchanges.
A number of these vulnerabilities will be considered in the LPA NRA and the VA NRA.
A number of the Island's TCSPs are part of wider Groups. In the Group of International Finance Centre Supervisors (GIFCS) Evaluation Report of IOM TCSPs it advises that TCSPs have been deemed not to represent a systemic risk to the IOM.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.3 TCSP Sector, 6.3.3.2 Inherent Vulnerability Factors for TCSP Sector to TF, RULE BOOK - 877d7e3ae61a1a1f

6.3.3.2 Inherent Vulnerability Factors for TCSP Sector to TF
body:
TCSPs that are part of Groups typically follow group-wide policies and procedures, the procedures must comply with IOM legislation. This includes the Financial Services Rule Book 2016 (Rule Book) .

Note 97: 2023 data included a one-off event which distorted the figures, so 2022 data is used

The Rule Book stipulates that every TCSP must appoint a:

- Head of Compliance with responsibility for overseeing the licenceholder's compliance with the regulatory requirements, including those relating to AML/CFT

- MLRO

- Deputy MLRO to cover the absence of the MLRO.

The same individual may be appointed as Head of Compliance and as MLRO or DMLRO. The Rule Book states that the Head of Compliance must: a) have appropriate independence and direct access to the licenceholder's responsible officers

- b) have unfettered access to all business lines and support departments

- c) have appropriate status within the licenceholder to ensure that the responsible officers react appropriately to recommendations

- d) have sufficient time and resources to discharge properly the responsibilities of the position

- e) be resident in the Island.

The Head of Compliance may report to a Group function, which is designed to share knowledge and provide a line manager with specialist risk expertise.

The Rule Book states that a licenceholder may not delegate any material management or business function without the consent in writing from the FSA. If activity is outsourced, to Group or elsewhere, the ultimate responsibility remains with the licenceholder for the delegated functions. The FSA has issued guidance on this rule to aid the sector. The guidance does cover outsourcing to Group entities:

" The FSA is more likely to consent to outsourcing to other Group entities. This reflects the degree of common systems, control and responsibility between the licenceholder and the service provider."

6.3.3.2 Inherent Vulnerability Factors for TCSP Sector to TF
body:
In the GIFCS Evaluation Report of IOM TCSPs it states:

" The FSA takes part in colleges and shares information regularly. It actively and timely responds to any gateway requests received from other regulatory bodies. The FSA confirmed that not all multi-jurisdictional TCSPs have had Supervisory Colleges, however the FSA has participated in 6 supervisory colleges and the IOM have 11 multi-jurisdictional groups."

Source: FSA AML/CFT Annual Returns

The Colleges provide the FSA with an opportunity to discuss a firm with other regulators.

The GIFCS Evaluation Report confirms their view that Group structures are effectively supervised in the whole and not solely at the individual level. The report states:

" The Rule Book provides for ownership structures for both IOM and non-IOM incorporated structures, with supervision undertaken whether at the solo level or if part of a group. The structural requirement places emphasis on ownership ensuring that at any given time; applicant, owners and even changes in ownership are made known to the FSA. Applications are accompanied by a structural plan with updated versions required, rendering the process expansive whilst catering for changes. There have been no examples where the ownership structure has hindered effective supervision. The Licencing Policy limits complex structures."

FSA08 prescribes the mandate and powers to the FSA. The FSA inspections methodology (October 2021) is also published. The most recent version of the FSA's supervisory framework was published in May 2023. The document details where the policies and procedures fit into the control considerations.
Through the publication of sector reports and the analysis of the AML/CFT returns (including financial flows from the banks) the staff within the FSA have a good understanding of the risks within the sector and in determining where to focus resources when devising the Engagement Plan.
Figure 6-23 shows the number of AML/CFT inspections and what prompted those inspections and thematic questionnaires with the TCSP sector since 2020. The figures indicate that there has been increasing engagement by the FSA with the TCSP sector.
In July 2023 the FSA issued a thematic questionnaire on the BRA to 106 TCSP licenceholders for completion. This was followed up with inspections which consisted of 70 desk-based inspections of TCSP licenceholders focusing on the BRA and their compliance with paragraph 5 of the Code. In addition to AML/CFT annual returns and supervisory inspections covering AML/CFT, the FSA holds discussions with the TCSP's internal audit and compliance teams and has meetings/dialogue with the IOM Association of Corporate Service Providers on matters where required.
In 2022 the FSA invited the GIFCS to review the supervision of TCSPs. The report assessed the FSA as 'compliant' (the highest rating) in 9 of the 10 categories and 'largely compliant' in 1 .
Source: FSA
3 Availability and Enforcement of Administrative Sanctions 0.8 Very High The FSA seek to:

- Intervene at an early justified stage in issues to help prevent unacceptable risks crystallising

- Understand, collaborate and follow a reasonable path of remediation to achieve the right outcomes

- Ensure enforcement is pursued where proportionate, reasonable and appropriate.
A full suite of regulatory measures is available and applicable including both criminal and civil penalties, including against individuals. Administrative sanctions include directions, conditions, suspension and revocation.
Various Acts overseen by the FSA enable the FSA to require a current or former licenceholder to pay a penalty for any contravention of the Act or any prohibition or requirement imposed under the Act. The Financial Services (Civil Penalties) Regulations 2015 came into effect on 1 August 2015. In 2019 the AML/CFT (Civil Penalties) Regulations were introduced.

Extensive criminal sanctions are in place for noncompliance with CFT obligations. These are detailed in ATCA with a maximum custody term not exceeding 14 years. headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Criminal sanctions are available for the substantive TF offences and for the failure to report TF offences. There have been no TF prosecutions for substantive TF offences. There has been a failure to report a suspicion of TF, investigation leading to a prosecution of two counts under s.14 ATCA in which the prosecution alleged that there was a failure to report (by someone working in a TCSP) in circumstances where there were reasonable grounds to suspect the financing of terrorism, giving rise to an obligation to report. For this offence to be made out, no terrorist financing needs to take place and in this case there was no admissible evidence that terrorist financing had taken place or was to take place. The issue was, had the Prosecution proved beyond reasonable doubt, that there were reasonable grounds for the TCSP employee to suspect that there may be TF and, on the evidence, were the elements of the offence triggering the reporting obligation made out. The Deemster ruled at the close of the Prosecution's case that there was not sufficient evidence upon which a jury could properly convict and the Deemster withdrew the two s.14 counts from the jury and directed them to return not guilty verdicts on those two counts.
5 Availability and Effectiveness of Entry Controls 0.8 Very High

The FSA's Licensing Policy for Regulated Activities under the FSA08 sets out the criteria that applicants must satisfy to be successful in securing and retaining a financial services licence. The FSA will not issue a licence unless it is satisfied that the licence applicant, including the persons associated with it, is a fit and proper person to undertake the regulated activity. The fit and proper test is both an initial test at the time of granting a licence and a continuing test in relation to the conduct of regulated activities.
The test considers integrity, financial standing and competence.
The FSA may be challenged in the Courts by an applicant if they do not agree with the FSA's decision. This was the situation in a recent (non-TCSP) case.
The FSA monitor entry controls and report on the vetting of individuals within the TCSP sector.
6 Integrity of Staff in the Sector 0.7 High
The level of integrity and the operating environment in the IOM is generally considered to be of a good standard. The sectors in the IOM with the largest firms benefit from additional in-built controls and checking. The IOM is also not considered to have significant issues regarding corruption/bribery of officials. There has been one recent example where the IOM based defendant was acquitted of his involvement in the bribery of a Ugandan official.

The FSA monitor data on the notifications of fraud, staff discipline and criminal convictions and report internally on an annual basis. They also track notifications of employee screening which may affect an assessment of the fitness and propriety of an individual.
7 CFT Knowledge and Awareness of Staff in the Sector 0.6 Medium High
First issued in 2006, revised on many occasions and most recently in 2022, the FSA "Training and Competence Framework" sets out the FSA's detailed expectations of its applicants, the regulated sector and their staff in relation to ongoing training and competence and should be read in conjunction with the "Regulatory Guidance - Fitness and Propriety". The framework is split into two distinct segments:

- PART 1: General Training and Competence Requirements - What the FSA expects of the regulated sector in relation to the training and competence of all staff

- PART 2: Controlled Functions and Other Functions - Training and Competence - the additional expectations applicable to individuals undertaking or aspiring to undertake certain Controlled Functions or certain other functions.
When applying the training and competence framework, an applicant/business in the regulated sector should consider the specific risks and needs of its business. Global bodies and agencies also issue helpful papers, manuals and videos such as the World Bank, FATF, MONEYVAL and others.
