The typical Life Insurance international typology is associated with ML threats rather than TF, such as:

- As an IFC with a large Life Insurance sector, the Island might be seen as a potential location for the proceeds of crime to be layered and then moved out for TF purposes

- The funding of insurance policies by third parties/persons different to the policyholder who have not been subject to the regular identification procedures when the insurance contract was concluded

- Typologies include those with more complex transfers of money via bank accounts or cheques through different jurisdictions, which complicates the control of the (legal) source of funds by the insurance company.
For the Life Insurance sector the customer base is almost all cross-border in nature, with 99.9% of personal customers being outside of the Island and 96.6% of non-personal customers. As at the end of 2023, in respect of the total customer base, 87.3% of customers were natural persons.

Life insurers cannot necessarily exit a client. The cash activity in this sector is zero. No life insurer receives or sends cash.
The sector broadly operates cross-border either via branch structures which are regulated and/or through regulated introducers. When operating branch networks, they will work to the same group standards, normally adopting the highest standard that applies (whilst complying with local laws and regulations). The country may have operational teams to support locally written business and a network of intermediaries such as Independent Financial Advisers (IFAs). Since COVID-19 restrictions were lifted, the IFAs may now distribute to a wider base as the use of technology is more readily accepted by customers.
IOM Life Insurers must comply with the Code, including paragraph 37 "branches, subsidiaries and agents". This means that the IOM Life Insurer must ensure that a branch or subsidiary takes measures consistent with the Code and guidance issued by a competent authority for AML/CFT. The guidance issued in the Island explains that:
" This does not mean that the measures must mirror those of the IOM in every detail, rather, that the measures should be of an equivalent or consistent standard to those in the Isle of Man.

The branch, subsidiary or agent is subject to the AML/CFT/CPF regime of the jurisdiction that it is established in and must ensure that it complies with this, including the reporting requirements of that jurisdiction."
As informed by routine supervisory oversight, the FSA observes that IOM Life Insurers that are themselves part of wider groups and/or operate through branches or subsidiaries abroad (as specified above), generally adopt standard policies across companies (jurisdictionally) and then modifications exist where there are more stringent regulations/ requirements in particular jurisdictions to which they would de-fault i.e. always to the higher standard. This ensures that Life Insurers are able to comply with all relevant legal and regulatory obligations, both for AML/CFT and wider Corporate Governance requirements.
The Life Insurers also have well-defined "3 lines of defence" governance structures in place in terms of ongoing monitoring and compliance and will also often operate a branch oversight committee as part of its overarching approach to governance within the Insurer.

In terms of onboarding and acceptance of money and settlement into life policy products, each Life Insurer that operates overseas branches will have its own approach as to delegation of authorities and corresponding levels of sign off/acceptance of business, which will often be in the IOM (subject to any outsourcing of activity). Legal entity-wide ongoing monitoring and screening processes, etc. will also be overseen by the IOM offices. The "in-country" presence of an Insurer in key markets can also help as a mitigant to the inherent vulnerabilities that may exist.
If the FSA undertakes an inspection of a Life Insurer for AML/CFT compliance it will review the business as a whole (including reviewing activity that may have been generated through overseas branches) and would consider elements such as the Insurer's BRA and CRA as it applies to its whole business. The Prudential Supervision Division of the FSA is also planning to conduct a series of governance-focussed inspections to Life Insurers that operate overseas branches to validate the FSA's current understanding of how those firms oversee and govern their branch operations more generally; this work is expected to commence in 2025 and is planned into 2026.
With the exception of one overseas branches, overseas branches of IOM authorised Llife Insurers are all in groups other than A & B listed countries.

Some of the Life Insurance firms are themselves part of much bigger groups with global operations and may also outsource some functions to group entities. There are also direct subsidiaries and other entities, summarised in Figure 6-29 below.
Long-term business, such as Life Insurance products are designed to financially protect the customer and related third parties, which may include the insured, the beneficiary(/ies) of the contract and the beneficial owners, against the risk of an uncertain future event such as death or critical illness. Life Insurance products can also be bought as investment or saving vehicles and to support estate planning or pension plans. The Island's long-term sector is predominantly unit linked investment insurance business.
The assignment of a policy has several legitimate benefits, but creates the potential vulnerability of being misused. A terrorist financier might collaborate with groups of otherwise legitimate individuals, such as business owners, to redirect claims on their insurance policies. The terrorist financier might agree to pay these businesses, potentially in cash or VAs, a percentage of any claim payments received that exceed the face value of the claims.

There are comprehensive laws and regulations regarding CFT. In the IOM the two key pieces of legislation relating to TF are ATCA and TOCFRA.
The Life Insurance sector is supervised by the FSA. The FSA issue and maintain the AML/CFT Handbook.
The Isle of Man's AML/CFT framework of legislation and guidance is drafted to meet the FATF AML/CFT standards. AML/CFT legislation as defined by the Code means:

- section 7 to 11 and 14 of ATCA

- part 3 of POCA 2008

- parts 2 to 4 of TOCFRA

- financial sanctions which have effect on the Island

- the Code.
The AML/CFT Handbook provides extensive guidance across a range of matters that are key to the sector.
The FIU also issues guidance on completing SARs, as well as providing feedback on the quality of SARs.
2 0.8 Very High
FSA08 prescribes the mandate and powers to the FSA. The FSA inspections methodology (October 2021) is also published. The most recent version of the FSA's supervisory framework was published in May 2023. The document details where the policies and procedures fit into the control considerations.

The FSA has been receiving AML/CFT annual returns data for the last 7 years which informs the risk-based approach to Supervision as well as informing sector reports which are published on the FSA's website. The use of technology (STRIX AML) has further streamlined this process and allows for the efficient analysis of risk producing a risk heat map of both sectors and individual entities.

Through the publication of sector reports and the analysis of the AML/CFT returns (including financial flows provided by the banks) the staff within the FSA have a good understanding of the risks within the sector and are confident in determining where to focus resources when devising the Engagement Plan.
Figure 6-30 shows the amount of inspections and thematic questionnaires with the Life Insurance sector since Q2 2021.
3 Availability and Enforcement of Administrative Sanctions 0.8 Very High The FSA seek to:

- Intervene at an early justified stage in issues to help prevent unacceptable risks crystallising

- Understand, collaborate and follow a reasonable path of remediation to achieve the right outcomes

- Ensure enforcement is pursued where proportionate, reasonable and appropriate.

Various Acts overseen by the FSA enable the FSA to require a current or former licenceholder to pay a penalty for any contravention of the Act or any prohibition or requirement imposed under the Act. The Financial Services (Civil Penalties) Regulations 2015 came into effect on 1 August 2015. In 2019 the AML/CFT (Civil Penalties) Regulations were introduced.
A full suite of regulatory measures is available and applicable including both criminal and civil penalties, including against individuals. Administrative sanctions include directions, conditions, suspension and revocation.
Figure 6-31 displays the limited number (two) and value of regulatory penalties that have been imposed on the sector (Source: FSA) since 2020.
Fi ure 6-31: Penalties Im osed on Life Insurers g p
Source: FSA
A decision to impose a discretionary civil penalty will be made by the FSA in accordance with the Enforcement Decision-Making Process. The Authority has published a Guidance Note to provide additional information on the operation of the discretionary civil penalties regime.
4 Availability and Enforcement of Criminal Sanctions 0.6 Medium High
Extensive criminal sanctions are in place for noncompliance with CFT obligations. These are detailed in ATCA with a maximum custody term not exceeding 14 years. For an employee of a Life Insurer the threat of criminal sanctions alongside internal disciplinary procedures and loss of employment are strongly dissuasive.

There have been no prosecutions or convictions for TF of Life Insurers to date.
5 Availability and Effectiveness of Entry Controls 0.8 Very High
The FSA's Licensing Policy for Regulated Activities under the FSA08 sets out the criteria that applicants must satisfy to be successful in securing and retaining a financial services licence. The FSA will not issue a licence unless it is satisfied that the licence applicant, including the persons associated with it, is a fit and proper person to undertake the regulated activity. The fit and proper test is both an initial test at the time of granting a licence and a continuing test in relation to the conduct of regulated activities. The test takes into account integrity, financial standing and competence.
The FSA may be challenged in the Courts by an applicant if they do not agree with the FSA's decision. This was the situation in a recent (non-Life Insurer) case.
The FSA monitor entry controls and report on the vetting of individuals within the sector.

Life assurance companies in the IOM are, in the main, subsidiaries of large internationally active groups head-quartered in the UK or Europe. The life sector consists of authorised and permitted insurers writing predominately long-term unit linked business, where policyholder liabilities are directly linked to the performance of an underlying financial asset.
IOM life companies are generally internationally focussed, targeting High Net Worth Individuals (HNWIs) and mass affluent customers, including expatriates and non-resident customers. The IOM domestic market is insignificant. Clients from certain geographic destinations, such as the Middle East and South America may give rise to increased suspicions of TF. Chapter 7.2.10 considers the threats from large-scale terrorist organisations.
The consistency in laws, regulations and supporting agencies does result in very similar controls to the Banking and TCSP sectors and hence a similar score. The quality of controls was deemed to be medium.
The overall residual TF risk was lower than Banking and TCSP sectors due to a number of factors including the low suitability of the products offered for TF purposes and fewer TF typologies for the sector.

PIMLIT and FIU have VA tracing capability. Through shared licences they are able to trace VAs linked to criminality including TF. This allows the agencies to trace through the blockchain, identify other lines of enquiry or touchpoints where assets are converted to fiat currency. The VA tracing licences give the capability for operational staff that identify seed words /VA wallets to be able to look up and identify assets or any markers/ red flags on the blockchain. Crypto tracing makes it easier to identify and trace cross-border movement of assets. This is a significant capability improvement to PIMLIT and FIU that can be applied in a TF-related financial investigation.
This capability allows LEAs to see where assets derive from and if they originate from frauds/US sanctions breaches and other activities which terrorist financiers might use.
The GSC have invested in both external and internal training programmes on VA risks including training on the use of blockchain analysis tools and explorers. Online gambling firms may have operations in jurisdictions apart from the IOM. It depends upon the business model; for example, if there is a large client base in a particular country, the firm may have operational/telephony teams in that jurisdiction. If there is a software supplier based in another jurisdiction then there may be other operational activities also in that third country. Almost none of the customer base is local, therefore almost all transactions are cross-border in nature.
Whilst the exposure to higher-risk countries has reduced markedly since Q2 2024, the exposure prior to Q2 2024 has been used for the rating, thereby assessing the exposure to higher-risk geographical locations as 'significant'.
Online gambling businesses also interact as customers and the Gambling (Anti-Money Laundering and Countering the Financing of Terrorism) Code 2019 (Gambling Code) includes additional requirements around customers acting by way of business. This could be a company that uses an algorithm to spot where a marginal return can be made usually over a long period or businesses that accept bets looking to hedge or lay off the bet with a bet of their own to cover losses.

The sector has, according to figures reported to the GSC through the STRIX AML platform, 0.02% very high-risk clients and 1.58% high-risk customers. A large amount of the sector's activities come from a high volume of customers making small value transactions.
The GSC undertook a review of the deposits held by the top 5 firms vs the overall sector. The top 5 hold the overwhelming majority of the deposits, highlighting that the risk presented by the Sector may derive from a small number of firms.
There are PEPs within the client book of online gambling firms, though the overall numbers are extremely low, as the majority of operators will not accept customers that are PEPs as a risk-based commercial decision.
There is no reliance upon third parties to undertake due diligence. All players must be onboarded by the Online Gambling firms. All online business is non-face-to-face (noting that terrestrial is in person, see Chapter 6.3.6.15): nor is it allowed to use introducers. It is difficult to use Online Gambling anonymously with any degree of success. It is possible to enter false details and commence gambling. Many sites offer facilities where a player can play games for free (albeit they cannot win money either). Fictitious names in free-play databases are common. However, the ultimate pay-out of any winnings or unused deposits must be to the original depositing instrument. That means that to gamble with money, the person must have registered with details that will pass checks a licensee makes on name, address and date of birth. These checks typically include screening on government or private databases and over a EUR 3,000 threshold (and normally at much lower levels) the supply of photographic ID and proof of address.
The use of VAs in any transaction increases the risk of that transaction from the GSC's perspective and their guidance informs operators to treat VA users as higher-risk and to apply stricter controls and lower thresholds.

A network services licence must be obtained if the operator wishes to allow one or more foreign registered players on to its IOM software server without re-registering the player details. The holder of a network services licence provides services to another operator (a Network Partner (NWP)) enabling the NWP's customers access to the operator's systems. The operator does not have a relationship with the player. Network Services are subject to supervision under the Gambling Code and additional licence conditions apply. Licence conditions require the operator to notify the GSC of new NWPs and enter into NWP agreements that establish contractual arrangements for AML/CFT controls. The GSC conducts checks on the NWP agreements and CDD conducted by the operator on the NWP but is unable to "look-through" to the underlying player. Specific AML/CFT Guidance for NWPs is planned for 2025.

It is current GSC policy that NWPs must be licensed in the relevant jurisdiction(s) to their operations where such a regime exists.

Given the reliance on the NWP which may be an unlicensed entity and the GSC's inability to oversee AML/CFT controls applied to the underlying player, this should be considered a weakness in the system.

Software Supply companies make games and sell them. They are licensed to provide games to GSC-licensed operators and have no gambling activity. They are exempted from the Gambling Code requirements as they are not DNFBPs under the FATF Methodology; they simply provide software to other gambling firms, they do not accept customers or customer funds. However, licence conditions do apply which require the operator to have mechanisms for reporting ML/TF suspicions and AML/ CFT Guidance for Software Suppliers is available on the GSC website. The GSC's ensures compliance with the Guidance through its supervision and inspection regime.
As with Network Services the GSC does not conduct checks on Software Supply businesses' customers (unless the services are being provided to a GSC-licensed B2C operator). It may be possible that an operator's software (i.e. games) are used for criminal purposes further down the chain as games can be sold and resold.

All licenceholders under OGRA are subject to the same level of entry controls, risk assessment, ongoing monitoring and supervision and risk-based inspection. 2 Effectiveness of Supervision/Oversight Activities 0.7 High
The GSC is the regulator that supervises the gambling sectors' compliance with legislation and regulations made under OGRA, associated guidance and licence conditions. The Gambling Supervision Act 2010 is the principal legislation that provides for the status, constitution and functions of the GSC.

body:
The GSC supervises compliance through a combination of self-assessments and on-site reviews. Desk-based reviews of self-assessments and any documents provided allow the GSC to assess an operator's policy and process. General Supervision is the division in GSC that is responsible for the oversight and supervision of operators from licence approval to licence cessation.
AML Supervision of licenceholders is outlined in the Gambling AML/CFT Act 2018:

- Conducting investigations into alleged breaches as necessary. Guidance for supervision inspections has been published for entities to review

- Ensuring operators submit quarterly returns that includes AML/CFT information including internal and external disclosures, financial flows per jurisdiction, etc

- Conducting on-site inspections to assess the extent to which the operator complies with the AML/CFT legislation taking into account the operator's own procedures for achieving compliance.
As at Q2 2024 the GSC had approximately 53 employees, with 17 ring-fenced staff who are focussed on AML/CFT engagements. The staff hold many relevant professional qualifications. All staff receive in-house and external training on gambling models. Average turnover is at about 5% per annum. The overall team has increased in recent years.
The GSC covers TF in their training for all staff and the inspection teams undertake International Compliance Association diplomas which cover TF.

3 Availability and Enforcement of Administrative Sanctions 0.7 High
The GSC publishes a number of policies to ensure there is a good understanding of each step of enforcement strategy and process. The policies are:

- Enforcement Strategy

- Referral for Enforcement Policy

- Enforcement Decision-Making Process

- Discretionary Civil Penalties

- Prohibition Policy

- Publication Policy

- Use of Appropriate Experts Policy

- Settlement Policy

- Referral for Criminal Investigation

- Guidance on the Audio Recording of Interviews

- Guidance for Individuals - Interviews Under Compulsion Powers

- Guidance for Advocates - Interviews Under Compulsion Powers.
Administrative sanctions include:

- Power to restrict holders of permits or licences

- Addition of licence conditions

- Directions to appoint an expert or to prohibit appointment

- Injunctions and remedial orders

- Civil penalties

- Warning notices and Public Statements

- Prohibitions

- Suspension or revocation of licences or permits.
There is a Register of Discretionary Civil Penalties which advises the firm that has been subject to enforcement action and the amount of the penalty imposed. Public statements are also made.

body:
Extensive criminal sanctions are in place for noncompliance with CFT obligations. These are detailed in ATCA with a maximum custody term not exceeding 14 years.
There have been no prosecutions or convictions for TF of Online Gambling firms to date.
The GSC do publish a document on how they make a referral to the police and/or AG, so there is clarity on both the process and risks of being prosecuted.
The GSC does not currently have the authority to sanction an individual. There is a plan for the GSC to be given this power.
5 Availability and Effectiveness of Entry Controls 0.5 Medium
Guidance for Making an Online Gambling Licence Application details the requirements that must be satisfied as well as the types of different licence that can be applied for.
OGRA gives the GSC Commissioners the authority to approve designated officials. There are accompanying forms and declarations that are required. There is guidance on procedures and controls, as well as on compliance officers and staff.
Within the GSC there is a standalone division with 12 ring-fenced staff who are tasked with undertaking entry controls at licence application and every 5 years from licensing. The team also undertake entry controls on any changes of shareholding or ownership. All entry control applications are put to the independent board of the GSC for a decision. Staff undergo training on carrying out CDD, open-source and adverse media alongside AML/CFT training and specialist training VA risks, PF, etc.

body:
The GSC require full details of beneficial ownership and control and the thresholds are set at 5% ownership for full EDD to be required. Below 5%, full CDD is required, but not additional diligence such as police checks. Open-source checks and ongoing screening for adverse media is in place for all owners and defined controllers such as directors, senior managers, etc. The GSC have a threshold set at 20% ownership for publicly-owned companies but can waive this at discretion under policy if there are concerns.
The GSC conducts ongoing monitoring for PEPs, sanctions and adverse media. Where criminal activity or adverse media is noted within licenceholders' wider groups, the GSC will consider in line with the regulatory framework the integrity of the owners and controllers. In a recent case in which a group company was associated with criminal activity, the GSC worked with partner agencies to suspend and remove the licence in order to cause disruption.

body:
Organised crime is sophisticated and it is the remit of a regulator to detect and prevent criminal activity where it is associated with licenceholders. As was outlined in the IOM 2020 ML/TF NRA, the threat posed 'by criminal ownership or misuse of a licence is significant. Criminal ownership of businesses associated with a regulated gambling entity would be significant'. This risk still remains and amendments to strengthen the controls are in plan to be drafted and added to the legislation, which will give the GSC additional powers. This risk is also identified in other NRAs, such as the Malta 2023 NRA which stated, 'Licensed institutions controlled by foreign criminal groups… the Italian police had announced that an entire online network of betting companies, part of which was headquartered in Malta, had direct connections to the 'Ndrangheta', a notorious Calabrian criminal organisation.'
A recent GSC public statement advising of the cancellation of a licence confirmed that the firm was no longer "under the control of a person of integrity".
The Online Gambling sectoral risk assessment will further assess the ML threat of criminal capture.
6 Integrity of Staff in the Sector 0.6 Medium High
The Guidance states that an operator must establish, record, maintain and operate procedures and controls to enable the operator to satisfy itself of the integrity of new officers and of all new appropriate employees and workers. It also outlines requirements on new staff appointments.

requirements, is in line with the business risks and is effective.

During on-site inspections the GSC do test understanding of TF knowledge during interviews/ testing. Across the sector, 10.2% of all staff received specialist TF training in addition to the annual training required.
8 Effectiveness of Compliance Function (Organisation) 0.6 Medium High
The risk-based approach requires that every policy links back to the BRA which must take into consideration the volume and nature of the business.
The Guidance requires that the Compliance Officer must have sufficient seniority and authority; they must also have sufficient time and resources to properly discharge their responsibilities for implementing and testing AML/CFT/CPF procedures and controls and reporting to the board.
The Guidance states that operators should consider commissioning periodic audit reports by an independent third party expert. Such reports can be helpful in providing an unbiased expert opinion from a fresh perspective. Such reports can be particularly helpful where it is not possible for the Compliance Officer to be completely conflict-free or where extra attention is required to fully understand and remediate shortcomings.

The Guidance outlines what is required for ongoing monitoring for occasional transactions and regular activity. This includes:

- a review of information and documents held for the purpose of CDD to ensure that they are upto-date, accurate and appropriate, in particular where that transaction or relationship poses a higher-risk of ML/TF

- appropriate scrutiny of transactions and other activities to ensure that they are consistent with:

- o the operator's knowledge of the customer, the customer's business and risk profile and source of funds for the transaction

- the BRA
o any relevant TRA

- the CRA

- monitoring whether the customer or any known beneficial owner is listed on the sanctions list.
Systems must be tested and reported on internally at least annually as mandated in the Gambling Code and tested on inspection by GSC.
As is the case for most sectors, staff would benefit from further training and awareness of typologies to increase their awareness of TF and hence increase the number of submitted SARs to the FIU.
See Chapter 7.1.20
Almost all of this sector's customers are not local to the Island. The firms are well versed in using screening and verification tools which link to public information systems for screening.
The firms also use tools to identify browser, type of device being used, model and operating system, detect use of VPN, as well as tools to identify for fraudulent documents.

Online Gambling firms in the Island are regulated and overseen by the GSC with supervision oversight extending to include CFT. The GSC is an independent statutory board of the IOM Government and was established in 1962. Whilst the laws and regulations differ from the sector supervised by the FSA, the CFT legislation applies to both and there is commonality in a number of areas including the Codes. This consistency, as well as the common reliance upon the same supporting agencies (including IOMC, FIU, AGC, Customs & Immigration, as well as others) does result in a number of similar controls to the Banking/TCSP/Life Insurance sectors and hence some similar scores.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.5 Online Gambling Sector, 6.3.5.4 Summary for Online Gambling Sector, ONLINE GAMBLING SECTOR OVERVIEW - 78807d3a9eda260e
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Recent ML investigations involving Online Gambling companies have prompted a reassessment of the adequacy and effectiveness of the GSC's previous entry controls in this area, resulting in a lower entry controls score. The GSC has identified a number of actions and measures to mitigate those risks. Efforts are in progress to establish a clear legal foundation for risk-based licensing decisions which are stricter than the standard entry control checks previously applied. The experience derived from these ongoing ML investigations in this area has been further considered as part of a multi-agency threat assessment. Overall, the quality of controls was deemed to be medium, although recent public statements by the GSC have indicated where certain controls require strengthening to ensure that the risk of TF is minimised in respect of any revenue coming through this sector. There have also been weaknesses identified in the B2B controls. A large amount of the sector's activities come from a high volume of customers making small-value transactions. Almost all the Online Gambling sector customers are international and not-face-to-face.
The inherent TF risk was assessed as medium.
Overall, the residual TF risk the Online Gambling sector is exposed to is medium.

Most premium outflows are to the reinsurance sector, much of which is placed in the London and Lloyds insurance markets. Significant claims generally involve the appointment of an independent loss adjuster who will verify the claim and advise on reserves and settlement values.

The Island offers a broad range of captive management services (see insurance managers above). Captives have become an integral part of the risk management strategy of many large companies and continue to offer one of the most effective and widely used mechanisms for risk treatment.

Authorised captive insurers have a larger cross-border exposure compared to other parts of the non-life sector, with clients (group entities) in circa 30 countries, noting more of a concentration to UK and South Africa. chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.1 Non-Life Insurance, RELEVANT LEGISLATION AND REGULATION - 8eb05550d961e812
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The FSA regulates the different parts of the non-life insurance sector. Non-life insurance companies carrying out insurance business in or from the Island are required to be authorised under the Insurance Act 2008. Insurance managers and general insurance intermediaries are required to be registered under the Insurance Act 2008.

Figure 6-45: Penaltiesand Fees Applied to the Non-Life Insurance Sector

There have been penalties applied to two firms in 2020 but none since then. The penalty in Q1 2020 was only partly for AML/CFT failings.

The FSA has issued sector specific guidance , which assists the non-life insurance sector which covers all 3 activities (General Insurance Intermediaries, Insurance Managers, Authorised Insurers and Permit Holders). The sector specific guidance does refer to kidnap, ransom and cyber insurance. It states that:

" The payment of a ransom (whether paid in fiat or virtual currencies generates proceeds of crime) and these proceeds may be used for terrorist or proliferation financing…. It is important that registered persons comply with the Code requirements in relation to external disclosures if they are involved in a ransom payment. Relevant persons should be aware that the payment of a ransom is illegal in some jurisdictions."

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.1 Non-Life Insurance, TF-RELATED MATTERS - 529fcbd840f53bff
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
There is a significant cross-border aspect to parts of the Island's Non-Life sector, most notably the captive insurance sector. The data also confirms that some business is conducted on a non-face to face basis through introducers. (Source: FSA AML/CFT annual return).

Higher-risk factors for the sector might be:

- applications from countries where there may be a closer and equally suitable country offering the same product

- where the rationale for insuring does not make sense

- seeking policies of a value that does not appear to meet the requirements

- customers that are legal entities whose structure makes it difficult to identify the ultimate beneficial owner.

The FATF Risk-Based-Approach (RBA): A Guidance for the Life Insurance Sector 2018 references non-life insurance and gives the following example as a typology:

"where non-life insurance products might be misused for ML and TF is the utilization of illicit funds for the payment of premiums or a significant overpayment of premiums followed by a refund request for the full amount or the amount overpaid."

Incoming and outgoing payments are almost exclusively bank transfers, with negligible cash accepted and no virtual asset transactions.

Overall, the residual TF risk the Non-Life Insurance sector is exposed to is estimated as medium low.

- As defined by FATF on its Virtual Assets web page :

- " Virtual Assets (crypto assets) refer to any digital representation of value that can be digitally traded, transferred or used for payment. It does not include digital representation of fiat currencies."
An NRA will be written for the Island for VAs , this will also consider the TF risk. Therefore, this Chapter provides a brief overview and does not seek to quantify the TF risk. Should the VA risk materially differ from this jurisdictional TF assessment, then it will be considered as a trigger event and this NRA will also be reviewed in the light of the additional information.
The registered VA/Virtual Asset Service Provider (VASP) sector in the IOM ranges from small VA issuers to international VA exchanges. The usage and purpose of each registered designated business is diverse and positioned within a rapidly evolving industry. The sector is largely international-based with non-domestic customers.
Digital IOM, part of the IOM Government, actively promotes the Island to Financial Technology (FinTech) firms. Its website states :

- " The Isle of Man's regulatory position has always been one that is tech agnostic, where it is the activity that is judged for regulation, not the underlying technology."

6.3.6.2 Virtual Assets and Virtual Asset Service Providers
body:
POCA schedule 4 defines VA activity. By virtue of being included in schedule 4 of POCA, VA/VASPs are subject to the AML/CFT Code 2019 and the Designated Businesses (Registration and Oversight) Act 2015 gives the FSA the power to oversee the sector for CFT purposes.

The Travel Rule (Transfer of Virtual Assets) Code 2024 was introduced in October 2024. This puts obligations on the relevant person who sends a VA to a VASP to obtain and hold certain information and where the relevant person receives a VA from a VASP it must ensure it has received certain information.

The GSC regulates gambling activities related to VAs and has issued AML/CFT Guidance for VA/Goods which provides guidance of the TF risks in VA and virtual goods and illustrates areas where further controls can help mitigate the risks. In addition, an operator must seek permission from the GSC before they accept VA deposits by any route.

Due to the nature of the rapidly evolving sector, particular focus should be given to the TRA. This must estimate the risk of ML/TF posed by any technology utilised by the business, such as the use of online delivery channels and communication methods, to its business. The BRA must also take into consideration the TRA.

FATF states on its Virtual Assets web page :

- " Without proper regulation, virtual assets also risk becoming a safe haven for the financial transactions of criminals and terrorists. The FATF has been closely monitoring developments in the cryptosphere and has issued global, binding standards to prevent the misuse of virtual assets for money laundering and terrorist financing. In recent years, some countries have started to regulate the sector, while others have prohibited virtual assets altogether. However, the majority of countries are yet to implement effective regulations. These gaps in the global regulatory system have created significant loopholes that can be exploited by criminals, terrorists and rogue regimes."
As at the end of 2023 the sector's customer characteristics were:

- Very few PEPs, with none from jurisdictions that may pose a higher-risk

- 55% of the PEPs were nationals and resident in the UK

- 0.2% of natural persons were resident in List B countries

- 81% of natural persons are resident in the UK

- There were no non-natural persons from List A or B countries

- 65% of non-natural persons are resident in the UK

- 1.4% of UBOs are from jurisdictions that may pose a higher-risk

- 68% of UBOs are resident in the UK.
In her paper New Technologies but Old Methods in Terrorism Financing , Jessica Davis writes:

" The most popular cryptocurrency among terrorists and extremists is by far Bitcoin, lauded for its supposed anonymity as well as the mythology surrounding its creation. Terrorists and extremists have used Bitcoin to move money and to pay for services like as webhosting, although terrorists (particularly the Islamic State) also use other cryptocurrencies like Monero. The most common terrorist use of cryptocurrency is to solicit donations from supporters."
Jessica Davis, New Technologies but Old Methods in Terrorism Financing
The sector is rapidly evolving globally and is also complex. The level of regulatory (and investigatory) expertise in the field is limited and this creates challenges in keeping up with developments. Also, with these services there is a level of anonymity available which is greater than traditional non-cash methods and difficulty in linking an 'account' to a real identity.
The sector has factors which increase the potential threat, including:

- Anonymity

- Global reach and disaggregation

- Near-real-time settlement and irrevocability of transactions

- Challenges in tracing and seizing assets.
The VA NRA will consider these and other threats and vulnerabilities.

There is one regulated Credit Union on the Island, Manx Credit Union Limited (MCU).

Information is provided to the FSA as part of the annual AML/ CFT return, which the FSA uses to assist with supervision. The MCU also provides quarterly and annual financial data to the FSA. However, no data, except that which is already public, is presented in this document, as it is not possible to aggregate or anonymise data for one entity.

The MCU promotes itself as providing savings and loans and is run solely for the benefit of its members. Members must be over 16 years of age and live on the IOM (noting provisions in place to deal with the situation when a member moves off Island). It is run by volunteers.

As of 30 September 2023 (published financial statements), the MCU had 1,431 members, with total assets of £1,435,555. The size is therefore determined to be very low.

headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Credit Union activity is included in schedule 4 of POCA, therefore the sector is subject to the Code and the FSA08 gives the FSA the power to regulate the sector and to oversee the sector for CFT purposes. A licence to carry on the Class 9 regulated activity of Operation of a Credit Union permits an entity that is incorporated as a credit union under the Credit Unions Act 1993 to operate a credit union in the IOM.

The Credit Unions Act 1993 provides tight restrictions on business. A member must be resident on the Island, may not have a shareholding of greater than £15,000 and the law allows a loan to be no more than £5,000 in excess of the paid-up shareholding. This restricts the business activity and consequential TF risk.

The MCU has participated in two AML/CFT-related thematic questionnaires and a business meeting with the FSA in 2024.

6.3.6.4 Collective Investment Schemes (Funds), Fund Managers and Administrators
body:
Fund managers and administrators in the IOM provide services to a range of fund vehicles, both IOM funds and overseas funds (which are subject to AML/CFT frameworks in their home jurisdictions). Whilst there are a number of IOM funds, most are private arrangements (i.e. exempt schemes).
The population of Fund Managers/Administrators varies in terms of the types and numbers of funds they provide services to. Some are focussed on only a small number of retail type funds, whereas others focus on servicing a wider range of clients including IOM qualifying funds, experienced investor funds, specialist funds and exempt funds, together with services to overseas funds or to overseas managers/administrators.
As of June 2024 (Source: FSA), Assets Under Management:

- Services to IOM schemes = USD 2.54bn ● Services to overseas schemes = USD 9.51bn
Both the IOM funds themselves and the fund managers/ administrators are subject to the AML/CFT framework.
Fund managers/administrators are responsible for assessing the ML and TF risk associated with taking on funds as clients. This includes an understanding of not only the investor base but also what the fund is investing in, the fund structure and the other functionaries providing services to the fund. The funds are responsible for complying with the Code, in relation to their clients, but in practice the governing body of the fund usually delegates this to the manager/administrator.

body:
The Fund Management /Administration sector is mature and is regulated under the current FSA08 legislative framework, with previous regulatory frameworks applying for over 25 years.

All funds established in the IOM under the Collective Investment Schemes Act 2008 are also "relevant persons" for the purpose of AML/CFT legislation; this means the AML/CFT Code also applies directly to IOM funds as well as the functionaries. In practice the governing body of an IOM fund will delegate the majority (if not all) of AML/CFT matters to its functionaries (fund manager/ administrator), but the governing body must understand and document what services the functionary provides and more importantly is not, providing in relation to the fund's obligations under the AML/CFT Code.

A licence to carry on the Class 2 regulated activity of Investment Business permits a firm operating in or from the IOM (within certain criteria and with specified exclusions) to:

- deal in investments

- arrange deals in investments

- manage investments belonging to another person

- provide administration and safeguarding of investments

- advise on investments.
Businesses that provide services to Collective Investment Schemes will need to hold a separate Class 3 licence.
Investment Firms' customers vary from retail and general corporate customers through to those that just support institutional customers.
Services under a discretionary mandate mean that the firm is trusted by customers to make appropriate investment decisions for them. An initial assessment is completed with the customer to work out investment objectives and risk appetite and then a strategy is planned to fit the customer profile and needs. The manager will then take charge of all investment decisions and, providing the appropriate documents are in place, will not require consent for transactions. Minimum investment levels tend to be higher than those for Financial Advisors.
Advisory investment management is more intensive and offered by larger firms and private banks. The wealth manager will advise on strategies for investment but the customer makes the final decision and or approvals.

body:
The sector consists of IFA firms with permission to arrange deals and provide financial advice to clients. In the majority of cases, Financial Advisers do not have permission to hold client monies or client assets.

The IFA industry presents a broad mix of potential risks driven by the inherent risk of the business, geography, services & products and customers involved. There are factors that can increase a firm's risk if not properly managed, including culture, insurance issues, poor controls around advice, underqualified persons giving advice, fraud, vulnerable clients, mis-management of conflicts and financial crime risks.

Typically, Financial Advisers give financial advice upon packaged retail products and pensions to domestic customers with whom they have direct ongoing contact.

The sector's client base is predominantly local resident individuals, with business conducted on a face-to-face basis. Due to the nature of services provided, Financial Advisory firms need detailed information about their clients' needs, their financial circumstances and must assess the ML/TF risk of the customer.

There is very limited reliance on third parties for CDD collection or the use of introducers. The sector uses the local banking system and no substantial reliance is placed on other parties outside the Island. Money being settled into an investment product recommended by an IFA will pass from one regulated business to another, but not to or from the IFA. Cash is only very occasionally accepted and never issued by the sector.

As a consequence of these risk mitigants, overall the residual TF risk the sector is exposed to is estimated as low.

body:
Money Transmission Services capture the broad areas:

- PSP and EMI

- Bureau de change, cheque cashing and payment services as agent.
The sector is small, in parts relatively new, but diverse in terms of business models. The risks of TF will therefore vary for each business based on a wide range of factors, such as the type of services and products they supply, their customers and delivery channels.
The sector may be involved in occasional transactions, which is predominant in respect of bureau de change and payment services as agent. There are 2 bureaux de change in the Island at present, one of which is the IOM Post Office and the other provides the service as ancillary to its main travel agency business.
Source: FSA
At the end of November 2024, there are 6 licensed money transmission firms - the change since the end of March 2024 is the surrender of one firm's licence (payment services as principal only) and the addition of 2 new firms (both payment services as principal and e-money).
The Island is seeing possible growth in the PSP and EMI sectors with around half of all new licence applications and enquiries in this sector alone.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.7 Money Transmission, THE SECTOR - 8393f6ddd002e9cd

body:
Money Transmission firms that conduct payment services as principal and e-money report data to the FSA as part of the annual AML/CFT returns. Given the small size of the sector, there is a comparatively small number of people working in the sector. In 2023 there were no staff vacancies which included compliance staff. All the staff received annual training and 37% of all staff received additional specialist training.
Money transmission firms that only conduct bureau de change, cheque cashing or agency business report annually to the FSA using a separate bespoke return. This includes AML/ to request and obtain information and are subject to the requirements of the Code by virtue of being included within Schedule 4 to POCA.
CFT information such as number and value of transactions by payment method, transaction thresholds, numbers of internal and external SARs, enquiries from competent authorities, training data, declined and terminated business and CRA data. In addition, for agency business the top 5 countries for money sent and received are reported (noting there are currently no firms operating agency business in the Island).
IOM Post Office also provides reports to the FSA annually (for bureau de change activity) or quarterly (for payment services activity).

headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
There is experience internationally of the use of money service providers to transmit funds for the purposes of acts of terrorism. There are features of the sector that might be attractive to a terrorist financier, including: simplicity and also the certainty of transactions; ability to send funds cross-border with ease; breaking transactions down into multiple smaller amounts to avoid detection (structuring); portability of products; ability to layer via several transactions; non-face-to-face.
The two Class 8(2)(b) money transmission agents have closed since the last NRA was published (including agency activity undertaken by the IOM Post Office). As a consequence the TF risk within the agency sector has proportionally reduced.
Figure 6-54: Case Study
The FSA in their Sector Guidance provide a case study for how the sector is used to finance terrorism.
A father and son held numerous prepaid cards, which were charged daily from all over Italy. Shortly after, the sums were withdrawn so that the cards' account balances were almost always close to zero.
EMI customers typically have low value and low volume of payments which are inherently higher-risk for TF as such payments will typically not be picked up by transaction monitoring processes, especially when undertaken as peer-to-peer payments.
Many of the PSPs and EMIs operate in higher-risk markets and jurisdictions which further increases their exposure to potential TF risk.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.8 Pensions, TF-RELATED MATTERS - 132b733984d4c8ab
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Generally, new members of a pension scheme in the sector are not met face-to-face by the Scheme Administrator. A common exception to this would be for domestic schemes established by local IOM companies (for the pension accrual of their employees) and for some bespoke schemes.
Payment into a scheme by way of physical cash is not accepted by this sector (as per annual AML/CFT return) and almost all transactions are via bank transfers.
Pension schemes tend to see funds inaccessible for long periods of time and do not generally offer the level of flexibility needed to be attractive for traditional TF purposes, although there is some flexibility as to when funds can be accessed from a pension. Examples of when funds/benefits can be taken are:

- When the member retires from employment (for nondomestic arrangements this can include leaving service of the employer and may not be age-restricted),

- When a member suffers from serious permanent illness,

- Once the member attains a certain age (usual minimum retirement age of 50),

- Benefits taken as a lump sum upon retirement.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.8 Pensions, TF-RELATED MATTERS - 4122ebdcacbac3ea
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Research of public documents identifies a number of possible typologies/red flags which could impact the sector:

- FATF report on Emerging Terrorist Financing Risks, October 2015 - an FTF, having travelled to a conflict zone, still takes benefits from their pension fund (noting that some FTFs may be retired)

- Council of Europe MONEYVAL typology research report, Money Laundering Through Private Pension Funds and The Insurance Sector, September 2010 - identifies a number of red flags for private pension schemes for ML, which might also apply to TF, including:

- Large sums deposited in Pension schemes by members of the scheme, particularly when followed by substantial withdrawals of funds

- Unrelated third-party paying contributions on behalf of a member of a pension scheme

- Unemployed person paying contributions into an employee pension scheme
Note 151: The employer will be the customer of the Scheme Administrator and the sponsor of the scheme. Their employees will be the members of the scheme.

- Funds or other assets deposited into a pension scheme which are inconsistent with the profile of the policyholder

- The type or volume of the transaction, which is untypical of the economic activity of the client and explanatory notes to transactions conducted by the client arise reasonable suspicion.

6.3.6.9 Accounting Profession: External Accountants, Tax Advisers & Payroll Agents
body:
The Accounting Profession sector consists of:

- External Accountants - who provide accountancy services to a third party. Activity 2 in Schedule 1 to the Designated Businesses (Registration and Oversight) Act 2015 (DBROA)

- Tax Advisers - who gives advice on a third party's tax affairs. Activity 3 in Schedule 1 of DBROA

- Payroll Agents - who are not the individual's employer, but is involved with the payment of earnings to or for the benefit of, any individual. Activity 4 in Schedule 1 of DBROA.
The Accounting Profession sector in the IOM ranges in size from sole practitioners to the offices of large international practices and provides bookkeeping, audit, tax and advisory services. Tax services, including advice on structures and the mitigation of tax liabilities, can be provided by accountants and tax advisers but also by legal professionals and in-house experts in TCSPs. Where a Payroll Agent undertakes calculations relating to tax it should be classed as a Tax Adviser. Figure 6-56 shows the crossover between designated business activities undertaken by firms in the sector as at the end of 2024.

The activities of External Accountants, Tax Advisers and Payroll Agents are designated under Schedule 4 to POCA as undertaking business in the regulated sector. DBROA brings the sector into the FSA's oversight for compliance with the AML/CFT Code purposes.
The Accounting Profession Sector firms on the Island are primarily locally focussed, although there are IOM branches of UK/Global firms.
As part of the 2023 AML/CFT annual return, the Accounting Profession Sector provide information on introduced business and for each introduced customer the jurisdiction of the introducer.
The FSA has delegated oversight agreements in place with a number of professional bodies; members of these bodies can elect to have the oversight of their AML/CFT compliance
The AML/CFT returns were analysed by introductions for the number of customers from: IOM; UK; European Union Countries; Higher-Risk Countries; Other Countries, which includes other IFCs. 28.4% of introduced business came from outside the IOM or UK, mostly from the EU. Only 0.5% from higher-risk jurisdictions. The FSA monitors introductions and their locations.

body:
The FSA recently published a thematic review of the Accounting Profession (External Accountants, Tax Advisers and Payroll Agents) registered businesses focussing on CRAs. The thematic review has allowed the FSA to gather further data, assisting in risk assessing both the firms and sector itself, as well as building knowledge and findings to feed back into the AML/ CFT Handbook and the AML/CFT sector-specific guidance documents. The CRAs are vital to helping the firm understand and evidence the risks which their customers may pose to the business of the firm. CRAs allow firms to identify those customers with higher-risk profiles, in order to apply appropriate procedures to prevent TF, as well as ML and PF. Detailed findings of the sector were included in the published report and firm-specific findings were provided in entity level reports.

The sector's role in facilitating the cross-border entry of businesses into a jurisdiction which is an IFC is recognised as a potential threat if these businesses are susceptible to TF.
The Financial Transactions and Reports Analysis Centre of Canada (FINTRAC) published indicators for accounting firms , including indicators specifically related to TF, including:

- Transactions involving certain high-risk jurisdictions such as locations in the midst of or in proximity to armed conflict where terrorist groups operate or locations which are subject to weaker ML/TF controls

- The use of funds by a NPO is not consistent with the purpose for which it was established

- Client-conducted travel-related purchases (e.g. purchase of airline tickets, travel visa, passport, etc.) linked to high-risk jurisdictions (including cities or districts of concern), specifically countries (and adjacent countries) under conflict and/or political instability or known to support terrorist activities and organisations

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.10 Legal Services, THE SECTOR - 7c315c79c5590321
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Legal professionals qualified to practice IOM law are Advocates; it is a fused profession and Advocates take the roles of both solicitors and barristers. The sector also comprises Registered Legal Practitioners. Registered Legal Practitioners are legal professionals qualified to practice law in jurisdictions other than the IOM who may work for IOM legal firms or who may be practicing the law of the jurisdiction in which they are qualified, but from the IOM.
Advocates provide the full range of legal services including wills and probate work, litigation, family law, criminal law, immigration law, corporate and commercial work and conveyancing. Registered Legal Practitioners may provide similar legal services but not in connection with IOM law. Only Advocates can appear in the IOM Courts and provide advice and assistance in relation to IOM law.
The Legal firms on the Island are primarily locally focussed, although there are IOM branches of UK/Global firms.
As part of the 2023 AML/CFT annual return, the Legal sector provide information on introduced business and for each introduced customer the jurisdiction of the introducer. The AML/CFT returns were analysed by introductions for the number of customers from: IOM; UK; European Union Countries; Higher-Risk Countries; Other Countries, which includes other IFCs. Only 7% of introduced business came from outside the IOM or UK and only 0.4% from higher-risk jurisdictions.
Source: FSA AML/CFT Annual Returns

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.10 Legal Services, THE SECTOR - 9119291312584be5
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
The nature of the services offered does result in a number of customers engaging with the sector for one-off transactions; for example the preparation and execution of a Will is a finite instruction, as is a conveyancing transaction. However, these transactions may then lead to a long-term relationship, allowing the advocate's firm to get to know their client extremely well.
There are a mix of law firms of varying size and some will have a greater international focus. Some firms will only undertake work within the IOM, for example conveyancing, where the risk profile is very low, given they may have known both parties and the property itself, from years of service on the Island.
Some law firms have a separate Trust and Corporate Service business, which would hold the relevant TCSP licences, whilst other firms pass business to the TCSP sector acting as an introducer.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.10 Legal Services, ADVOCATES, Relevant Legislation and Regulation - 93707045549eb8c5
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
Advocates are included in Schedule 4 to POCA. DBROA brings the sector into the FSA's oversight for compliance with the Code purposes.

Activities captured under POCA include: managing any assets belonging to a client; the provision of legal services which involve the participation in a financial or real property transaction.

Firms can choose who provides oversight in respect of AML/ CFT between the FSA or the IOM Law Society (Advocates only). The IOM Law Society has oversight of AML/CFT for the majority of the firms. The IOM Law Society has a compliance team which undertakes support and advice, oversight inspections and testing; copies of all inspection reports are provided to the FSA. In addition, the FSA holds regular meetings with the IOM Law Society to discuss inspection findings and trends within the sector. The FSA retains its power to inspect those businesses overseen by the IOM Law Society. In some cases there may be joint inspections by the FSA and the Law Society.

Legal professionals who are providing 'in-house' services as an employee of an entity that does not fall within the definition of a legal professional are not included in Schedule 4 to POCA or required to register under the DBROA.

Legal professional privilege does not negate the obligations placed on Advocates to comply with the AML/CFT legal framework and submit SARs.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.10 Legal Services, TF-RELATED MATTERS - 7c0444e111e7abe7
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
In common with most other sectors, the awareness of TF risks is thought to be slightly lower than for ML, therefore further TF training, typologies and outreach is recommended.
In the FATF report Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Vulnerabilities of Legal Professionals published June 2013 it highlighted key ML/TF methods that commonly employ the legal sector as being: use of client accounts; purchase of property; creation and management of companies and trusts; setting up and managing charities.
The majority of customers are met face-to-face, although approximately 10% are remote. The Acceptable Applicants concession is used within the sector.
Cash/virtual assets are rarely/never accepted by law firms.
The Manx legal services sector has close links with the UK. Therefore, the UK ML/TF NRA was reviewed to support this assessment. The UK rated the Legal Services sector as low in 2017 and 2020 for TF. It stated:
" The risk of terrorist financing through legal services is low. We continue to assess that legal services are not attractive for terrorist financing and there remains no evidence of these services being abused for terrorist financing purposes."

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.10 Legal Services, TF-RELATED MATTERS - f5f1fe5e9114d567
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
International organisations (such as the FATF/MONEYVAL), through various reports, typologies and guidance, do not consider the Legal Services sector as inherently vulnerable to TF itself. However, the Legal Services sector's role in facilitating the cross-border entry of businesses into a jurisdiction which is an IFC is recognised as a potential threat if these businesses are susceptible to TF. The sector also supports other sectors with the establishment of structures which could unwittingly be used for TF purposes. The sector may be attractive to a terrorist financier, as its professionalism provides credibility that third parties seek.
The sector is less likely to be at risk of TF from domestically focussed legal work, nor from legal services which are typically provided in one-off transactions rather than long-term business relationships. As a result, the chances of unwittingly establishing business ties with individuals from jurisdictions that may pose a higher-risk and thus facilitating terrorist financing, are low.
The sector assists charities and consequently there is a threat where the charities operate and send funds outside of the Island and there are connections with jurisdictions that may pose a higher-risk. This threat will be covered further in the NPO TF NRA which will be published in early 2025.

Registered Legal Practitioners who are qualified in another jurisdiction can practice the law of the jurisdiction in which they are qualified from the IOM provided that they register as a Registered Legal Practitioner. Registration does not enable the Legal Practitioner qualified in another jurisdiction to practice or advise on IOM law. Only Advocates can practice and advise on IOM law.

Registered Legal Practitioners are registered individually. Estate Agents in the IOM are involved in the buying, selling, renting and property management of residential and commercial properties. The sector is small, consisting in the main of wellestablished firms. The majority of the work undertaken is domestic; purchase of property and land outside of the IOM is most often dealt with by the TCSP sector, via property agents in the UK and elsewhere.
The term Real Estate Agent is defined by FATF:

- " A real estate agent should be broadly understood as a professional that operates within the real estate sector and is involved in transactions for a client concerning the buying and selling of real estate."
There are currently 20 registered Estate agents, which accounted for £533m of transactions in 2023.

In the FATF report Money Laundering & Terrorist Financing Through the Real Estate Sector published in June 2007, it gives various examples of typologies, including cases where terrorists have used non-financial professionals or gatekeepers to access financial institutions. A case study was given in the report:

- " A trustee for a trust established in an offshore centre approached a real estate agent to buy a property in Belgium. The real-estate agent made inquiries with the bank to ask whether a loan could be granted. The bank refused the application, as the use of a trust and a non-financial professional appeared to be deliberately done to disguise the identity of the beneficial owner. The bank submitted a suspicious transaction report. Following the analysis of the financial intelligence unit, one of the members of the board of the trust was found to be related to a bank with suspected links to a terrorist organisation."

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.11 Estate Agents, TF-RELATED MATTERS - 24833f86ff6c2f71
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
In the FATF report on Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing Vulnerabilities of Legal Professionals published in June 2013, it identifies a number of TF typologies within the Real Estate sector, including:

- Intricate loan structures or credit arrangements being set up to obscure the origin of the funds

- Estate agents being used in their capacity as non-financial professionals to help facilitate transactions and obscure the true ownership of properties

- The use of shell companies or companies to purchase property and hide the true beneficiary

- Manipulating the value of a property to move illicit funds through successive sales and purchases.

The overwhelming majority of customers of the sector are met face-to-face. In the FSA thematic report, it was noted that 19 of the 20 estate agents collected CDD directly from the customer and not via a third party agent, therefore overall resulting in a lower risk due to the direct involvement with the customer.

Source: FSA AML/CFT Annual Returns

Funds (with the exception of rental payments) are not handled by Estate Agents; sale and purchase of property requires the involvement of Advocates who provide the conveyancing services and FIs, which further mitigates TF risks.

Overall, the residual TF risk the Estate Agent sector is exposed to is estimated as low.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.14 High-Value Goods Dealers, THE SECTOR - 0915662b668a49e1
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
High-Value Goods Dealers (HVGDs) are businesses that deal in goods and services of any description which involve total cash payments (one-off or linked transactions) which are equivalent to at least €15,000. The term "total cash payment" is not defined in legislation, however the following instances should be considered:

- a single cash payment of €15,000 or more

- several cash payments totalling €15,000 or more, including a series of payments and payments on account within a 90-day period

- cash payments totalling €15,000 or more which appear to have been broken down into smaller amounts to potentially come below the threshold limit.

- cash paid by a customer totalling €15,000 or more in any 90-day period
High-value goods of any type may apply, however these are likely to include businesses such as:

- art dealers

- auctioneers

- car dealers

- jewellers

- precious metal or stone dealers.

- Year (as at 31st March): No. of Registered HVGDs; Year (as at 31st March): No. of Registered HVGDs; 2020: 2; 2021: 1; 2022: 1; 2023: 1
The high-value goods themselves tend to be transportable, internationally exchangeable and easy to trade anonymously. Precious metals and stones are particularly attractive to terrorists because they have a high intrinsic value, are readily accepted across the world and gold can be melted down into many different forms.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.14 High-Value Goods Dealers, THE SECTOR - ab1592d6bcd5593e
headers: 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level
body:
In July 2015 FATF published a report into Money Laundering/Terrorist Financing Risks and Vulnerabilities Associated with Gold . In the report it highlights:

- It provides a mechanism for organised crime groups to convert illicit cash into a stable, anonymous, transformable and easily exchangeable asset to realise or reinvest the profits of their criminal activities and

- The gold market is a target for criminal activity because it is highly lucrative.
In February 2023 FATF published a report Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Art and Antiques Market . In the report it states:
" The trade in art, antiquities and other cultural objects is a billion dollar industry. It is one where individual objects can attract high prices and where there is a culture of privacy and discretion regarding the identity of buyers and sellers. The market has attracted criminals, organised crime groups and terrorists who seek to launder proceeds of crime and fund their activities. The use of cash, third party intermediaries, shell companies and other complex corporate structures in relevant transactions also represents relevant illicit finance vulnerabilities."
The report covers TF threats in this market and also highlights the threats associated with cultural objects, the involvement of terrorist organisations as well as transnational organised crime groups who cooperate with the terrorist groups to acquire, smuggle and sell the objects.

HVGDs are included in Schedule 4 to POCA. The activity is defined as dealing in goods or services of any description (including dealing as an auctioneer) whenever a transaction or series of linked transactions involves accepting a total cash payment (in any currency) that is equivalent to at least €15,000. By virtue of being included in POCA, high-value dealers are subject to the Code. The FSA oversee firms for CFT purposes. Therefore, any HVGD must be registered with the Authority in advance of accepting cash payments that total €15,000 or more. Businesses carrying out such activity without being registered commit a criminal offence.

The FSA has published specific guidance for this sector.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 6. TF Threat, 6.3 Step 3: TF Threat & Vulnerability at Sectoral Level, 6.3.6 Other Sectors, 6.3.6.15 Terrestrial Gambling, RELEVANT LEGISLATION AND REGULATION - 234b511138640fc1

There are various pieces of legislation including the Gambling (AML/CFT) Act 2018 ; The Casino Act 1986 ; Gaming, Betting and Lotteries Act 1988 The Gambling Code. The GSC supervises the sector. It provides AML/CFT Guidance for Gambling Operators , updated August 2024. The GSC splits customers into those where there is an ongoing relationship and those where there are occasional transactions however an ongoing relationship must be formed at a threshold. The requirements differ for these two categories of customer.
The Gambling Code requires all terrestrial gambling operators to identify the customer and the source of funds. A €3,000 threshold (stakes and winnings) applies; the operator must verify a customer's identity using reliable, independent source documents, data or information. The GSC has regularly undertaken inspections of the casino and 3 bookmakers.
Transactions are usually conducted on a face-to-face basis and on a time-sensitive basis. Cash is accepted, however it is often Manx notes - (see Chapter 7.1.3), which are more difficult to exchange outside of the Island.
There are 9 domestic PEPs within the sector (Source: GSC). Domestic PEPs have a much lower risk profile to Foreign PEPs and are not seen to carry any enhanced risk of TF.
