chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.1 Quality of CFT Policy and Strategy, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.6 MEDIUM HIGH - d5bcafb9a29f743f
headers: 7.1.1 Quality of CFT Policy and Strategy
body:
The Competent Authorities and the roles that they play in mitigating risk within the Island are detailed in Appendix 5 in the National Financial Crime Strategy. This also includes details of the governing boards that oversee Financial Crime in the Island, from:

- Council of Ministers

- Economic and National Strategy Board

- Financial Crime Strategic Board (FCSB)

- AML/CFT/CPF Advisory Group.
Appendix 5 includes membership.
The FCSB's purpose is to provide an effective mechanism to enable IOM Government, regulators and LEAs to coordinate the development and implementation of actions related to combatting ML/TF/PF and other financial crimes. FCSB is made up of senior officers from law enforcement, regulatory authorities, the AGC and the FIU.
The AML/CFT Policy Office team within the Cabinet Office was established by the Chief Secretary in 2016. The Policy Office: leads the Island's engagement with key international organisations such as MONEYVAL and reports back across the Island; provides advice to FCSB and the Chief Executive and politicians; drives the engagement across industry; leads on NRAs; coordinates international inspections of AML/CFT; and develops and delivers the anti-bribery and corruption project and National Financial Crime Strategy.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.1 Quality of CFT Policy and Strategy, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.6 MEDIUM HIGH - 10ceabea71afada4
headers: 7.1.1 Quality of CFT Policy and Strategy
body:
The Island is fortunate to have never experienced a terrorist attack. The IOM works with the CTPNW. IOMC maintains direct liaison with the CTPNW in relation to extremism and is linked directly to the CTP Network with access to the National Common Intelligence Application in respect of the reciprocal sharing of intelligence. Senior Officers are vetted to the appropriate level for direct interface with the Security Services where this may be required.
The capacity in the IOM for dealing with the terrorism threat is additionally reinforced through a close working relationship with UK authorities, which would provide extra capacity if needed, in the case of a terrorism incident on the Island.
As documented in CONTEST: The United Kingdom's Strategy for Countering Terrorism (2023), the UK has responsibility to the CDs stemming from international law and the constitutional relationship. The UK would support any locally-led response if a terrorist incident occurred. The IOMC primarily engages with the UK Counter Terrorism network through the 'Pursue' and 'Prevent' strands. If there were a terrorist situation with a primarily external nexus (UK based/affecting the UK/international), the UK National Crime Agency or the British Security Services would be the lead agency for identification and investigation and the IOM agencies would support.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.1 Quality of CFT Policy and Strategy, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.6 MEDIUM HIGH - 561ee731b7fd5968
headers: 7.1.1 Quality of CFT Policy and Strategy
body:
The FATF Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment Guidance (2019) emphasises "the importance of establishing regular mechanisms to monitor TF risks on an ongoing basis." The National Financial Crime Strategy confirms that the Island will conduct "an NRA underpinned by sectoral and focussed risk assessments and addressing the risks identified on a bi-annual basis". It is recommended that the NRAs will be reviewed every two years, to identify if there are any material changes that need to be reflected in the NRA. The NRA will also be reviewed on a trigger event basis if there is a substantive local or domestic event that impacts the TF risk to the Island or if the Island Plan/National Financial Crime Strategy require an NRA to be reviewed. Via FCSB, recommendations will be made as to which sectors to be reviewed or existing risk assessments that require to be refreshed (at least on a 5-year cycle).
Businesses in the regulated sector are obliged (under the Code) to undertake and update a BRA, which "assists relevant persons to understand where, how and to what extent they are exposed to ML/TF risk and which areas of their business they should prioritise in combatting ML/TF." A BRA must have regard to any relevant findings of the most recent NRA relating to the Island. Therefore, industry must be able to show how they have considered and mitigated the relevant risks identified in this NRA.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.1 Quality of CFT Policy and Strategy, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.6 MEDIUM HIGH - 9039d22ce81e4c36
headers: 7.1.1 Quality of CFT Policy and Strategy
body:
The National Financial Crime Strategy states in strategic objective 4 to"Ensure that our supervisory authorities are empowered and appropriately resourced to inspect, detect, investigate and, where appropriate, sanction instances of non-compliance with ML/TF/PF preventative measures." The agencies have received significant additional resources over recent years to assist in countering ML/TF/PF risks. In common with other smaller IFCs, there is a limited resource pool and competition across industry, agencies, regulators and Government for individuals with specialist skills.
Given the proportionally smaller size of the agencies compared to larger countries, then the key person risk becomes more apparent.
Following the increased resourcing to the competent authorities, it is recommended that more of the processes that cross several agencies are mapped to better understand the handovers and how the end-to-end process might be improved.
There are a number of pieces of legislation that are being updated/drafted which will enhance the quality of the CFT policy across the Island, including but not limited to the Financial Services (Miscellaneous Amendments) Bill.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.2 Effectiveness of TF Crime Definition, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 1.0 EXCELLENT - c95f55fb1c874591
body:
In the IOM the two key pieces of legislation relating to TF are: ATCA and TOCFRA. The legislation comprehensively defines the TF offences. The penalties are deemed to be proportionate and sufficiently high to be dissuasive, with a custodial term of up to 14 years for a TF offence.
The AG has recently published a Prosecution Policy and Guidance on TF Prosecutions internal guidance policy. The prosecution policy sets out:
" Guidance for TF offences in the IOM and the approach to be taken in considering whether a prosecution should be brought or not. The policy is to ensure that the principles and practices being considered in relation to TF prosecutions are underpinned by core values and to ensure a consistent and vigilant approach is taken relating to the prosecution of TF offending".
The AG notes in the policy, "It is acknowledged by the AG that opportunities for prosecutions in the IOM for TF offending are rare. Such investigations and prosecutions are by their very nature complex and present unique evidential difficulties that all prosecutors would need to carefully consider."

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.2 Effectiveness of TF Crime Definition, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 1.0 EXCELLENT - 937228a7e68ef87b
body: As is the case in a number of similar jurisdictions, the exposure to terrorism and TF is extremely low and therefore it is not unusual that there are few investigations/prosecutions and convictions. Given the recent publication of the Prosecution Policy Guidance on TF Prosecutions, it is recommended that the IOM undertake an Island-wide scenario test of how the agencies and regulators would approach a real TF case. This would allow a theoretical test of the current extensive laws, policies and procedures, communication mechanisms and data flows/information sharing gateways to be tested. The FATF Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment Guidance published in July 2019 provides suggested approaches and hypothetical scenarios. Other smaller jurisdictions have run these scenarios and their experiences and learnings will support the exercise.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.3 Effectiveness of Customs Controls on Cash and Similar Instruments, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.6 MEDIUM HIGH - 42e632f71d52c2c1
headers: 7.1.3 Effectiveness of Customs Controls on Cash and Similar Instruments
body:
The IOM is surrounded by sea and its nearest neighbours are the UK and Ireland. The overwhelming majority of the flights or ferries are to the UK or Ireland. As the greatest proportion of the Island's business is with or via, the UK, the overwhelming proportion of its passenger and traffic movements are to and from the UK and the Island is extremely closely linked to the UK. Checks are conducted on foreign parcels arriving in the Island at the Post Office. The IOM agencies have very close links with their UK counterparts.
Given the small population in the IOM, it consequently has limited expatriate populations from high-risk areas, who might send money back home. There is no evidence that underground Banking systems exist on the Island. The IOM is not a cash-based economy.
Customs & Immigration (C&I) Notice 9011MAN (updated 2024) titled "Carrying cash in and out of the Isle of Man" , covers cash, postal orders, travellers cheques, cheques, stored-value cards, coin or token with monetary value, banker's drafts, bearer bonds or bearer shares. This applies to cash going to or coming from, anywhere outside the Island, and regardless of whether the cash is being carried by someone or is sent in the mail, by courier service or is contained in freight, a vehicle or a vessel. The Notice includes the offences and penalties connected with cash controls.

Note 182: Following the recent name change from Customs & Excise to Customs & Immigration the names are used interchangeably in this document
Figure 7-3: Challenges by Officers at the Isle of Man Ports
The Customs and Excise Management Act 1986 (The 1986 Act) provides the powers to detect the physical cross-border transportation and Officers can ask questions at random or where they have identified someone to ask. The 1986 Act requires declarations of cash which exceed £10,000 on inbound and outbound movements. There have been recent cases where cash has been detected.
The 1986 Act informs all passengers regarding the limitations on transportation of cash, effectively enforces the declaration and disclosure requirements and allows the seizure of cash.
The resources allocated to C&I to control the borders has increased. They are aided by a specialist K9 team, including cash detection. As the number of challenges by officials has increased, displayed in Figure 7-3, the number of cash declarations in Figure 7-4 has also increased. It is assumed that there is a direct correlation.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.3 Effectiveness of Customs Controls on Cash and Similar Instruments, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.6 MEDIUM HIGH - ffef8ec4c343f976
headers: 7.1.3 Effectiveness of Customs Controls on Cash and Similar Instruments
body:
In common with the other CDs is the challenge of locally-issued IOM bank notes being taken cross-border by criminals and Organised Crime Groups (OCGs) and paid into banks in the UK and then being repatriated to the Island, a recent example being where an attempt to smuggle cash in a toy was intercepted. This issue was referenced in the 2023 Jersey ML NRA (section 7.16.6): "The FIU is currently working on a strategic report regarding Jersey notes being repatriated back to the Island as they are not legal tender in the UK." This matter was also referenced in the 2023 Jersey TF NRA (3.22). This vulnerability is continually reviewed by LEAs.
Training has been undertaken of border staff, but it is recommended that further training to enhance understanding of TF should be considered. This is a general theme across a number of staff within agencies. The expert judgement of the professionals from key agencies was that whilst training has been completed on TF, the level of knowledge was potentially still behind that for ML.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.4 Effectiveness of Border Controls on Goods (incl. military and strategic goods), 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.7 HIGH - bd95b04ee6b775ca
headers: 7.1.4 Effectiveness of Border Controls on Goods (incl. military and strategic goods)
body:
There are limited customs barriers between the Island and its closest neighbours and no fixed border controls to check the movement of people. This is a consequence of:

- the Island's constitutional status as a CD of the British Crown

- the establishment in law of the CTA which protects free movement of people between the UK, the Republic of Ireland and the CDs

- the customs union between the Island and the UK under the Customs and Excise Agreement 1979 which governs the customs controls on the movement of goods between the Island and the UK.
Under the Customs and Excise Agreement, the IOM and the UK are considered to be part of the same customs territory. This Agreement has existed for many years. Where there is a cross-border movement of goods between the Island and UK, this movement is generally not subject to customs controls - this is akin to the movement of goods between the mainland of the UK and Scottish Islands and Isle of Wight. There are however certain goods which are prohibited (banned) or restricted (i.e. require a licence, authorisation or declaration) from being imported or exported . The C&I Division is responsible for the enforcement functions at the Island's border.
There is a small manufacturing industry in the Island, the majority of which do not trade in military or strategic goods. Due to the logistics of getting goods on and off the Island, the Island is not a favoured place for manufacturing.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.4 Effectiveness of Border Controls on Goods (incl. military and strategic goods), 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.7 HIGH - 32df7839c93f2d2c
headers: 7.1.4 Effectiveness of Border Controls on Goods (incl. military and strategic goods)
body:
The Island uses the UK customs declaration systems and procedures so there is reliance upon the effectiveness of the UK border controls. However, as described elsewhere in this document, the Island is not a transhipment or trade hub and the majority of goods move between the Island and the UK, where there are established business links especially in the manufacturing industry.
C&I have an Export and Trade Controls webpage with specific information about strategic goods and firearms to guide business[187.] An export licence is needed before the export of controlled military goods, software and technology and items on the dual-use list from the IOM to any country other than the UK. These items are listed in Schedule 2 and 3 to the Export Control Order 2008 .

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.4 Effectiveness of Border Controls on Goods (incl. military and strategic goods), 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.7 HIGH - 6f200c756620fdb7
headers: 7.1.4 Effectiveness of Border Controls on Goods (incl. military and strategic goods)
body:
A trade control licence is needed before engaging in certain activities that involve:

- the supply or delivery of certain items from one country to another

- the agreement to supply or deliver certain items from one country to another Most export control and trade licences are available via SPIRE (UK Department for International Trade), the Export Control Joint Unit's online export licensing system. Export licences issued by the Export Control Joint Unit relating to IOM applicants indicate that controlled goods are being exported from the UK rather than directly from the IOM. C&I and the Export Control Joint Unit have a Memorandum of Understanding and engage on matters relating to export controls involving IOM businesses.

- any activity that will promote the supply or delivery of certain items from one country to another.
It is recommended that further training is considered for the Customs officers to better understand what to look for to identify military or strategic goods.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.5 Effectiveness of Immigration Controls, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.4 MEDIUM LOW - aba3788ffa66a9cf
body:
The Treasury formally took responsibility for Passports, Immigration and Nationality (PIN) services in January 2024. The Customs and Excise Division was renamed the Customs & Immigration Division, combining the customs and excise service and PIN services and is designed to improve efficiency and effectiveness through shared resources and personnel.
The Immigration Act 1971 (of Parliament) provides the statutory framework law for immigration control. This Immigration Act (as extended to the IOM) confers powers on the Minister for the Treasury of the IOM to exercise immigration control in the Island. Among these powers is the power to make Statements of Changes in Immigration Rules which are laid before Tynwald. The statement sets out the practice to regulate the entry and stay of persons subject to immigration control in the IOM and specify the conditions under which leave to enter and leave to remain may be granted and cover, visits, study, work, family reunion, removal and deportation. The Treasury Minister authorises officers to exercise the powers conferred on them by section 33(6) of the Immigration Act 1971 (an Act of Parliament as it has effect in the Island) and appoints an officer under paragraph 1 of Schedule 2 to the Immigration Act 1971 as an Immigration Officer to carry out the provisions of the Immigration Acts and any rules made under them.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.5 Effectiveness of Immigration Controls, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.4 MEDIUM LOW - d986759b38b1a671
body:
Geographical, natural borders help to prevent illegal crossings. The UK's departure from the EU has resulted in CTA, EU, European Economic Area (EEA) and Swiss national passenger arrivals to the Island now being under Immigration Control. This has increased the workload for the C&I teams.
The Chief Minister has recently stated (7 March 2024) that a firmer immigration policy for the IOM is being developed . The Chief Minister stated whilst giving evidence to Tynwald's Economic Policy Review Committee: "tightening up immigration policy would need to be developed within the next 12 months".
The Chief Minister also put this in the context of the wider Island strategy to increase the population by 15,000 to 100,000 by 2037.
It is important that national immigration legislation is compatible across the CTA to prevent any one constituent part of the CTA acting as a 'backdoor'. Notwithstanding, the IOM has a degree of autonomy in respect of its immigration policy, enabling it to adapt to local immigration and labour needs.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.5 Effectiveness of Immigration Controls, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.4 MEDIUM LOW - b89b91f8d6b21769
body:
Plans will be put in place to allow information and intelligence from all sea and air routes coming into and from the IOM to be gathered in a central hub/system. This central hub will allow the sharing of information with relevant enforcement agencies to enhance the understanding of the vulnerabilities; help maximise intelligence opportunities; develop evidence-based understanding of the CTA threats; enhance collaborative working; disrupt and deter terrorist and criminal exploitation of the CTA. This will result in an improvement to the quantity and quality of the information and intelligence collected which in turn will allow for more efficient and informed investigations to be carried out by the Island's enforcement agencies.
The IOM workers visa process could potentially be abused by criminals in two typologies.

- 1) A Visa is issued for a job that actually does not exist on the island and the person is effectively a modern slave, working long hours for illegally low pay.

The Financial Intelligence Unit Act 2016 (FIU Act) created the FIU as a 'Body Corporate'. The FIU has been a member of the Egmont Group since 31/3/2000 and is currently part of the Europe II region. As highlighted in the Egmont Group report the Role of FIUs in the National Risk Assessment Process , 'FIUs play a key role in analysing SARs and other data which provides critical insight in identifying TF risks within the country'.
The FIU has access to numerous closed databases both domestically, UK nationally and via open source. It makes requests of the regulated sector, government, other Egmont Group FIUs, International Anti-Corruption Coordination Centre (IACCC) and the Financial Crime Information Network (FIN-NET) and Beneficial Ownership requests.
Over recent years the FIU has had significant investment from the Government and the resourcing has increased. All FIU staff receive TF training. Additionally, the FIU has two Financial Intelligence Analysts who have been allocated TF as a specialism and primarily deal with incoming TF matters and receive additional dedicated TF training. The investment in people is supported with training and professional qualifications.

The FIU manage the SAR process. It works effectively using Themis and high-level SAR data is made publicly available. In August 2023, the FIU introduced a new feature into Themis to allow the provision of standardised feedback to MLROs on submitted disclosures. The Guidance document was updated in June 2024 on making SARs and disclosures to help industry, as well as a Good Practice document. These are all part of a suite of guidance documents provided by the FIU to industry .
Received SARs are subjected to FIU operational analysis to add value, which may involve consideration of the content and quality of the received information, its timeliness, local or international enquiries, analysis and interrogation of available open and closed sources. The FIU will then make a decision on which international and domestic partners would value from receiving a dissemination. Common recipients of FIU disseminations include domestic law enforcement agencies, regulators and FIUs in other jurisdictions All of the actionable TF SARs (or any SAR possibly linked to TF) received by the FIU were immediately developed and referred to PIMLIT for investigation as appropriate. Following initial enquiries, one of the referrals was adopted by PIMLIT as a criminal investigation. Following investigation, PIMLIT found that no crime had occurred. The overall number of such disclosures may appear to be low, however it is broadly in line with the low TF risk of the Island.

It also incorporates a proactive capability utilising financial and other intelligence to target TF activity. As referenced in 7.1.7, the Police have invested additional resources in PIMLIT, as has the AG in ICART.
The Police found they had spent time trying to locate bespoke TF courses and specialist training. Much of what is available is aimed at industry rather than agencies. To support this, the FIU have signed up a number of the agencies, for specialist TF training.
ICART is a Directorate of the AGC. ICART includes the Asset Recovery Unit, which identifies, restrains and recovers criminal assets in the IOM. ICART, on behalf of the AG, has conduct of all MLA requests made by and sent to, other jurisdictions in relation to criminal investigations and prosecutions, including obtaining evidence, restraining assets in the IOM and enforcing confiscation orders.
ICART is dedicated to MLA and Civil recovery action, to include civil investigative orders. The mirror image structure in FCU deals with criminal investigative orders and there is a very high degree of cooperation between the two units. This provides for a cohesive rapid response to TF threat and to criminal activity across the board.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.9 Integrity and Independence of TF Investigators, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.9 CLOSE TO EXCELLENT - c6c75daeffa63ec1
headers: 7.1.9 Integrity and Independence of TF Investigators
body:
The main legislation that covers bribery and corruption in the IOM is the Bribery Act 2013. The Bribery Act makes it an offence to: give or receive a bribe, bribe a foreign public official or fail to prevent bribery. There is also a duty under the Bribery Act for certain individuals to report bribery. The AGC prosecutes all crime in the IOM, including crimes involving bribery or corruption.
There is also an independent police complaints process.
There has been no prosecution for a substantive terrorist financing offence on the Island because none have been detected. There has been a failure to report a suspicion of TF investigation leading to a prosecution of two counts under s.14 ATCA, (see Chapter 6.3.3.3). There is no reason to consider that TF investigators would act with anything other than integrity and independence.
There is no reason to consider that a TF investigation would be the type of investigation where investigators might come to be pressurised or influenced by those who might conceivably be considered to be in a position where they might potentially seek to bribe or bring pressure on those conducting any TF investigation.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.9 Integrity and Independence of TF Investigators, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.9 CLOSE TO EXCELLENT - 5d5f1cd04bbacf3f
headers: 7.1.9 Integrity and Independence of TF Investigators
body:
The conducting of TF by a politician or member of the law enforcement/prosecution agencies is not a typology encountered in similar jurisdictions to the IOM. There have been no instances where any criminal investigators or prosecutors have been corrupted or bribed nor has there been any attempt to do so in relation to any offence, nor for any TF offence. Persons in elevated positions on the Island have been investigated and prosecuted in the past (for offences wholly unconnected with TF) and there has been no suggestions that such investigators and prosecutors have acted with anything but integrity and independence. Examples of such investigations and prosecutions include the following:

- An Attorney General was prosecuted for (and acquitted of) perjury in the past

- On rare occasions, police officers have been prosecuted and convicted for offences of dishonesty where they have stolen assets which have been seized. Police officers have been prosecuted in the past for other offences such as harassment

- The wife of a previous Chief Minister was prosecuted and convicted for a dishonesty offence in the past.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.10 Capacity and Resources for TF Prosecutions, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.7 HIGH - 3c8098a1d802f912
headers: 7.1.10 Capacity and Resources for TF Prosecutions
body:
The Prosecutions Division provides advice to the IOMC and other public authorities on potential criminal charges and the prosecutors make decisions on behalf of the AG in relation to criminal prosecutions. Within the Prosecution team there is a dedicated FCU in the AGC. Prosecutions are split into a general team and the FCU, which helps to increase specialism. FCU was established in 2024 and is a ring-fenced resource. FCU is structured to allow for procurement of specialist services and advice from a KC, as most prosecutions will be highly complex and lengthy. PIMLIT and ECU automatically come to the FCU - there is guidance for the other agencies on what may come to FCU.

Procedures allow the Prosecution team to seek KC from the UK. This is usually for cases which are very complicated or there are extreme levels of resource required. The Chambers runs all cases, with KC support.

The AG has issued the Prosecution Policy and Guidance on Terrorist Financing Prosecutions to support the prosecutors.

It is planned to update the Justice Reform Act 2021 which will streamline a number of the court processes.

There is a lower understanding across industry and the agencies of TF compared to ML, which impacted the overall score.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.11 Integrity and Independence of TF Prosecutors, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.9 CLOSE TO EXCELLENT - 344967c1c4835a45
headers: 7.1.11 Integrity and Independence of TF Prosecutors
body:
The AG was appointed by Her Majesty the Queen in 2022, a process which is independent of the Island's political system. The AG is not a politician and not subject to any party whip or collective responsibility. The AG can only be removed by the King (not the case in the UK) and therefore there is less scope for political pressure to be applied to the AG.

Safeguards to preserve prosecutor integrity are found in the Advocate Practice Rules 2001, which specifically applies the English Bar Code of Conduct and the Law Society (of England and Wales) Regulations. The prosecutors are also subject to the Advocates Disciplinary Tribunal which is a body established under Part IV of the Advocates Act 1976 to consider complaints against Advocates. The independence of the prosecutors from political interference and intimidation and abuse of office can be evidenced by the investigations, prosecution and convictions of influential people as outlined in Chapter 7.1.9.

FCU within the AGC, with the support of the AG, make the decision to prosecute TF cases. There are checks and balances in the prosecution process. All prosecutions are subject to Crown Officers being able to review. The decisions of Prosecutors may be judicially reviewed, as they are public officials. This is the situation as demonstrated by Bell vs HM Solicitor General & Others May 2024.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.12 Capacity and Resources for Judicial Processes, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.7 HIGH - 57bbd5ab4fe2f5d4
headers: 7.1.12 Capacity and Resources for Judicial Processes
body:
The IOM is a separate jurisdiction to the UK and as a result has its own legal system. The principles of the Manx legal system are based on English common law and the Island follows very closely the precedents set by the English Courts if there is no conclusive Manx precedent already established. However, Manx law has also developed to fit the IOM's own needs and circumstances, particularly in relation to tax, company law and financial supervision issues. The main sources of Manx law are based on the Acts of Tynwald and their subsidiary legislation .
The IOM's High Court judges are called 'Deemsters', who have jurisdiction over all criminal and civil matters on the Island. The first Deemster is the head of the IOM judiciary. The Island also has its own Magistrates, whose roles are similar to their English counterparts. There is a local Court of Appeal called the 'Staff of Government Division'. Since January 2015, Channel Islands Judges are eligible to sit as Appeal Judges in the IOM and IOM Judges are eligible to sit as Appeal Judges in the Channel Islands. The final Court of Appeal is the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in England.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.12 Capacity and Resources for Judicial Processes, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.7 HIGH - 7e965a7844f24369

body:
The number of judges has increased from 5 to 6 recently. The judges are able to call upon experienced UK Judges such as (His Honour Judge) Michael Hopmeier, who is a Circuit Judge (appointed July 2009) sitting at Southwark Crown Court, specialising in serious economic crime and confiscation. There is also one full-time circuit judge on the panel (His Honour Judge Kainth) and a further specialist financial crime KC (Simon Farrell KC) who deals with financial trials.
The Justice Reform Act 2021 (Appointed Day) (No.3) Order 2024 makes provision for trials without a jury in complex fraud cases, which increases the Court's capacity to hold trials quickly in appropriate venues, provided there is provision for electronic provision of evidence. It is planned to update the Justice Reform Act 2021 which will streamline a number of the court processes.
It should be noted that one of the risks identified in the General Registry 2023 annual report , is the recruitment and retention both judicially and administratively.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.13 Integrity and Independence of Judges, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 1.0 EXCELLENT - cb226b69997d0dc8
body:
There is a Code of Conduct for members of the judiciary in the IOM . The Code of Conduct is based on the six Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct which are well recognised internationally and which are concerned with (1) judicial independence, (2) impartiality, (3) integrity, (4) propriety, (5) equality of treatment and (6) competence and diligence.
The Rt. Hon. The Lord Garnier KC produced an extensive paper dated March 2023 of his independent review of the provision of legal services on the IOM .
The judiciary in the IOM is independent and has excellent levels of integrity. Appointments to the judiciary are through an open and transparent selection process. Candidates need to evidence significant legal experience as well as competency, integrity and independence requirements. The First and Second Deemsters and the Judge of Appeal are appointed by His Majesty the King on the recommendation of a recruitment panel. The judges are not political appointments.
All court proceedings are recorded and all judges are required to give reasons for their decisions. Manx judgements are available online and also through the published Manx Law Reports. There is a publicly documented process in respect of complaints of personal misconduct against members of the judiciary of the IOM.

The Council of Ministers Act 1990 section 6A and 6B cover the duty of the Council of Ministers to uphold the law and the independence of the judicial process.

Although there is strict application by FIs of the common law duty of confidentiality in respect of customer information, it is overridden by various statutory provisions including POCA/ATCA and others.
The framework for inter-agency cooperation serves as a factor for mitigating potential TF risk. The small size of the jurisdiction may be an advantage. There is no difficulty in prompt communication between authorities themselves and between the authorities and the private sector. Close collaboration across the jurisdiction is formalised in a number of forums, including:

- The AML Group consisting of Police/FIU/ICART/FSA/GSC and other agencies where required (such as C&I/Income Tax Division(ITD)) meets fortnightly to discuss intelligence on specific cases and then act upon it

- There is a team from PIMLIT (Case Development Unit) co-located but entirely separate in the FIU and they meet the FIU weekly. The Police receive good intelligence from the FIU, therefore it was decided that it would be more efficient, as the resources in PIMLIT were increased, for a small number of people to be in the FIU, although firewalls are in place. This has helped ensure that agencies work together in line with operational priorities and identified national risks

- There is the Joint Tasking and Coordination Group, which coordinates and prioritises the national response to specific cases enhancing overall cooperation between the law enforcement agencies.

body: The FIU has also been instrumental in the establishment of the IOM's PPP, the IOMFCP. Competent authorities have access to numerous international cooperation mechanisms through which the LEAs can exchange information both spontaneously and upon request. There is a central register of beneficial ownership that meets international standards, which helps to share information with authorities around the world. The IOM is:

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 7. TF vulnerability, 7.1 Step 4: National TF Vulnerability, 7.1.16 Availability and Effectiveness of TF Asset Forfeiture and Confiscation, 2025 ASSESSMENT: 0.7 HIGH - 2913e37929e23ed9
headers: 7.1.16 Availability and Effectiveness of TF Asset Forfeiture and Confiscation
body:
Section 16 of ATCA enables the forfeiture of "any money or other property" related to terrorism offences. The forfeiture orders can be made where the defendant is convicted of terrorism offences (sections 7 - 10 of ATCA) and that the money or other property, at the time of the offence, was in the possession or under the control of the defendant. The court may order the forfeiture of the money or other property which:

- a. had been used for the purposes of terrorism

- b . intended to be used for such purposes

- c. where the defendant knew or had reasonable cause to suspect that it would or might be used for those purposes.

Payments and rewards received wholly or partly, directly or indirectly,1 in connection with the commission of the terrorism offences are also subject to forfeiture under section 16(7).

It is planned that POCA will be updated, which will improve a number of aspects including confiscation, as well as Unexplained Wealth Orders.

The asset forfeiture policy is being updated for approval by the AG. Although not in relation to TF matters, various assets have been confiscated including crypto and properties.

Since the 2020 ML/TF NRA, the Island has not conducted any TF prosecutions or convictions and therefore has not had the opportunity to forfeit or confiscate assets related to TF activities. No alternative measures have been required or applied.

TOCFRA implements in law the targeted financial sanctions measures under UNSCRs 1267, 1373, 1718, 1988, 1989 and 2231. Although the IOM is not a UN member in its own right, the UK's membership of the UN extends to the Island; therefore the IOM is obliged to implement such measures. Where a person is designated under a UNSCR described above, that person automatically becomes a designated person under TOCFRA without any legislative delay and is subject to the asset freezes provisions listed below.
TOCFRA Sub Division 3 - Offences in connection with designations covers situations relating to:

44. Freezing of funds and economic resources

45. Making funds or financial services available to designated persons

46. Making funds or financial services available for benefit of designated person C&I is the competent authority for sanctions in the IOM , and its responsibilities include:

47. Making economic resources available to designated person

48. Making economic resources available for benefit of designated person.

- Implementing United Nations and UK sanctions legislation

- Publishing sanctions designation updates and guidance

- Providing outreach to promote compliance and prevent breaches of sanctions law

- Processing applications for and issuing, sanctions licences

- Working in partnership with other government agencies to monitor compliance with sanctions legislation

- Enforcing sanctions law in the IOM in conjunction with the IOMC.

body:
When the UK implements its own counter terrorism targeted financial sanctions under the Sanctions and Anti-Money Laundering Act 2018 (SAMLA), these measures also have effect in the Isle of Man by virtue of the Sanctions (Implementation of UK Sanctions) Regulations 2024. A person designated by the UK has effect in the Island. Where a person or entity is delisted, either by the UN or UK, the delisting has automatic effect in the IOM and the funds and other assets are unfrozen.
Law is in place should the Island decide to designate a person independently of the UK designating them (section 18 of TOCFRA). However, procedures to implement the law are not in place and it is recommended that they are written.
The IOM Aircraft Registry, as well as the Shipping Registry, implement sanctions. The speed and effectiveness of the processes within the two registries were evidenced when Russia invaded Ukraine.

TOCFRA ensures that the obligation to freeze, without delay, the funds or other assets belonging to a UN-designated person is met. Under the UNSCRs, there is an obligation to freeze all funds, financial assets or economic resources of designated persons/entities.
Where the UK Secretary of State or HM Treasury has designated a person under SAMLA for the purposes of UNSCR 1373, that designation also has effect in the IOM from the same time and any variation or revocation of the designation will also have effect in the IOM. The criteria for designation in the UK is if persons are or have been involved in terrorist activity. The UK Sanctions List states the people designated under the UK Regulations and details of the sanctions in respect of which they have been designated (e.g. asset freeze, travel ban, etc).
Communication of TFS designations made by the UN or UK are sent via a news release published on the Sanctions and Export Control website (which can be subscribed to) and further disseminated by the FIU and regulators through their own communication channels. Statistics are held by C&I which demonstrate how quickly these are issued compared to when the information is received or found from the UN or UK. In the majority of cases, IOM news releases are published within 24 hours of the UN publication.

The IOM does not require citizens to carry identity cards. The IOM is an issuing authority for British Passports. IOM variant British passport applications are processed in the IOM and printed in the UK by HM Passport Office at a secure facility in the UK to ensure the security and integrity of the passport. IOM Driving Licences are issued by IOM Post who is the licensing agent for the Department of Infrastructure. The IOM has an Electoral Register.
LEAs have experience of IOM-issued driving licences being a feature of a number of their investigations. There is scope for the processes for issuance of driving licences to be reviewed.
The absence of formal border controls within the CTA means that there is no mandatory obligation to check the identification of persons entering and leaving the IOM and travelling to or from the UK, Channel Islands and Ireland.
Particularly for the banks, the most common form of photo ID is a Government-issued passport or IOM driving licence. A framework is in place to deal with persons who may not have these documents (e.g. elderly, students). The AML/CFT Handbook provides extensive support and guidance to industry on CDD. Some banks also use electronic ID data tools for customers resident in certain countries, most commonly the UK as it is considered robust data sources exist there.

headers: 7.1.22 Availability and Access to Beneficial Ownership Information
body:
The Beneficial Ownership Act 2017 places all IOM corporate and legal entities under the same legislation regarding beneficial ownership. There is a central database for the recording of beneficial ownership of legal persons. The database went live July 2017.
Section 4(1) of the Beneficial Ownership Act 2017 defines "beneficial owner" as:

- " a natural person who ultimately owns or controls a legal entity to which this Act applies, in whole or in part, through direct or indirect ownership or control of shares or voting rights or other ownership interest in that entity or who exercises control via other means and 'beneficial ownership' is to be construed accordingly".
The Beneficial Ownership Act was amended by the Beneficial Ownership (Amendment) Act 2021. Some of the key changes were:

- A reduced period of 21 days for changes to beneficial ownership or nominated officers to be notified to the Central Registry

- A reduced period of 21 days for disclosure of beneficial ownership information by nominated officers

- Powers to make enquires to establish the accuracy of information and to remove, correct or annotate information which it considers to be false, inaccurate or misleading.

The Beneficial Ownership Act requires every legal entity (to which it applies) to appoint a 'nominated officer' unless the legal entity is in receipt of corporate services comprising Class 4 regulated activity provided by a TCSP, who may undertake the role or responsibility for which a nominated officer is responsible.
The Beneficial Ownership Act defines a registerable beneficial owner as someone who owns or controls more than 25% of the beneficial ownership of a legal entity to which the Beneficial Ownership Act applies. Therefore, there are instances where no one person owns more than 25%, yet someone/some people are controlling the entity, e.g. directors. TCSPs still have to identify and hold information on the beneficial owners with less than 25% beneficial ownership. The LEAs do have powers to obtain this information.
The FSA has oversight responsibilities to ensure the Beneficial Ownership Act is complied with and the nominated officer or TCSP complies with their obligations under the Act. It is a criminal offence not to comply with the Beneficial Ownership Act. Guidance is published by the FSA in order to assist firms with their obligations.
The Exchange of Notes (EoN) between the UK Government and the IOM Government in respect of the sharing of beneficial ownership information is available.
The Governments of the CDs issued a joint press release regarding registers of beneficial ownership of companies.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), Small States, 7.2.1 Introduction - cb9599830f8171c1
body:
Effective measures to address TF can only be put in place if the risks are understood. This can be a challenge for smaller financial centres, such as the IOM which is an IFC. Whilst the terrorist threat within the Island is very low, the main risk that exists to any IFC is if it is used as a transit jurisdiction for the movement of funds linked to terrorist activity in another jurisdiction. There is also a risk of becoming involved in the funds associated with people or businesses that are associated with terrorist activity.
There are several challenges:

- An extremely limited number of cases to study and competent authorities who consequently may have little experience of TF activity. This challenge has been identified as a central one for small jurisdictions, leading the IOM authorities to invest significant resources in addressing this issue: the creation of specialist teams (PIMLIT within the IOMC and FCU with Prosecution); additional resource within the FIU; additional resources within the FSA for both AML/CFT and Enforcement Divisions; additional resourcing for the GSC AML/CFT team; AG issuing internally the Prosecution Policy and Guidance on TF Prosecutions

- The difficulty in identifying potentially very small sums for which there is a terrorist purpose, versus the large sums required to maintain the terrorist entity

- The difficulty of assessing a risk that exists in another jurisdiction.

From the analysis of the TF risks arising in other IFCs there are a broad range of risks raised including:

- complex structures, which are briefly discussed in Chapter 7.2.4 and will be considered in the LPA NRA

- VAs will be considered by a separate NRA that is shortly to be produced

- NPOs are a concern in several IFCs and a separate NRA covering TF risk is being produced for the IOM considering the position for the Island.
The risks outlined in Figure 7-15 contain some elements that are encountered globally:

- Proving the payments are destined for terrorist activity - this is a common challenge globally regardless of IFC status, although is particularly prevalent in jurisdictions whereby the terrorist activity occurs internationally (such as in IFCs)

- Complex structures - the nature of business in IFCs tends to result in the presence of complex structures.
As part of the strategic financial flow analysis, the FIU and FSA will consider the flows from the Island to IFCs in a similar way to the analysis with financial flows to higher-risk jurisdictions.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), Small States, 7.2.2 Financial Linkages, EXPOSURE UK ELECTRONIC MONEY INSTITUTIONS - 334628649c434a7c
body:
In the March 2022 publication "Together in Electric Schemes: Analysing Money Laundering Risk in E-Payments" , Transparency International highlight that the UK is home to more than 260 EMIs and noted that a further 77 foreign EMIs offered services in the UK. The assumption is that a number of IOM residents will be using some of these service providers.
The report highlights the growing body of evidence that suggests that some of these EMIs are open to abuse by those seeking to launder corrupt funds and consequently could be disguising funds being moved for TF purposes.
In addition, as identified in the Dutch Banking Association: Financial Crime Threat Assessment of the Netherlands 2023 -24 , EMIs help create a fragmentation of the payment landscape.

- This threat arises from the increasing diversification of payment options, which can lead to widely dispersed regulated financial transactions

- Criminals can deliberately use the fragmented payment landscape to disguise money flows and make it more difficult to follow transaction flows

- Additionally, due to this increased fragmentation, law enforcement agencies may struggle to obtain a full view on financial flows and patterns and banks may find it challenging to understand the background of batch payments received from PSPs. This evolving landscape adds another layer of complexity to the already challenging task of transaction monitoring and financial crime detection.

body: Displacement risk is where business moves from one jurisdiction to another. This may be due to the tightening of controls, external factors such as sanctions or a country deciding their appetite for business from a particular industry/country/sector has changed. It is assumed that criminals exchange information with each other on the controls of a country and seek out the country with lower mitigating controls. The media widely reported the movement of Russian money to other jurisdictions following the imposition of sanctions in 2022.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), Small States, 7.2.3 Trade Linkages - 76c787efd4321f47
body:
There is very little manufacturing in the Island, due to the logistics of getting goods off the Island. The Island uses the UK customs systems and procedures so there is reliance upon the effectiveness of the UK border controls.

The IOM is an IFC rather than a trading hub. This is in common with the following statement taken from the Monaco Guidance:

- " Similarly, for IFCs without a significant manufacturing and trade sector, import and export of goods that could be used for terrorist purposes or used to finance terrorist activities is unlikely, although the possibility of IFCs being used as transit countries for such goods should not be overlooked (especially in the case of IFCs that are free ports or with ports which have significant entrepot activity with a range of other jurisdictions)."

In the TF NRA WB methodology, Step 1, Chapter 6.1 of this document, consideration was given to the terrorist risk from the two closest neighbours: UK and Ireland. Their TF NRAs were reviewed for guidance and typologies. Almost all trade is with the UK , which publishes UK import and export data, although there is no corresponding IOM data with which to compare with the UK published data. In the UK data the Island was the UK's 75th largest trading partner in the four quarters ending Q4 2023 accounting for 0.1% of UK trade. Almost all trade is in services.

body:
Due to their position, foreign PEPs might be targeted for corruption and bribery attempts and ultimately for money laundering or terrorism financing activities. Being a foreign PEP does not automatically mean someone is involved in criminal activities. However, their status enhances the threat that is posed and the enhanced due diligence measures that a firm must put in place to manage the relationship.
Whilst PEPs may be motivated by the desire to move money to an IFC, to shelter it for their and their families' personal gain, there is also the possibility that the proceeds might be used for state-sponsored terrorism. This is of greater risk where the PEP is linked to a higher-risk jurisdiction.

The FSA does examine customer files relating to PEP customers during supervisory inspections and has fined three regulated business for: not always identifying; identifying at the appropriate time; having documented customer risk assessments; having sufficient source of wealth/funds evidence for Foreign PEPs. chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), Small States, 7.2.6 Foreign PEPs, 'WHITE-COLLAR' TF THREAT - 6d831be76b08daaf
body:
This is the threat from HNWIs contributing to TF operations through donations, which are conducted by more sophisticated financial channels and instruments. In the IMF's Current Developments in Monetary and Financial Law Volume 4, Jeff Breinholt writes in the Chapter on Reaching the White-Collar Terrorist: Operational Challenges , published in 2008:

- " White-collar professionals - doctors, lawyers, bankers, academics, journalists - came to the United States to raise funds for violent organizations with which they were associated. During this era, some of the most lethal terrorist organizations operating in the world, like the Palestinian Liberation Organization (PLO) and the Irish Republican Army (IRA), raised a significant portion of their operating budgets in North America."

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), Small States, 7.2.6 Foreign PEPs, 'WHITE-COLLAR' TF THREAT - 68f850e5b4632fc1
body:
As an IFC, the IOM has many customers who are HNWIs in a number of sectors. In addition, some of these customers may also be in jurisdictions close to those where there is a higherrisk of terrorism. HNWIs may also be involved in activities which FATF has identified as being at risk of TF, as explained in the FATF Report - Money Laundering and Terrorist Financing in the Art and Antiquities Market, published February 2023 :

- " The market for cultural objects has a history of privacy and discretion. This protects sellers and buyers from being targets of theft or other crime and helps ensure that high net-worth individuals are not charged at a higher price if their identities is known to the seller. This may create vulnerabilities in terms of countering the risk of ML/TF, for example, where cultural objects can be purchased anonymously in cash, it complicates the traceability of transactions. The use of intermediaries and legal persons in the buying and selling process is relatively common in the market, which in certain cases can act to obscure the identity of the ultimate seller or purchaser."

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), Small States, 7.2.6 Foreign PEPs, 'WHITE-COLLAR' TF THREAT - 83bb96f02e8cb4be
body: In addition to HNWIs, Family Offices could potentially contribute to terrorist organisations. In the RUSI Occasional Paper: Examining the Unknowns: Money-Laundering Risk in the UK Professional Services Sector , published in 2019, the risk of "family offices or individuals acting as intermediaries on their behalf" is examined. The FSA published a paper on Family Office-Type Services in 2024 , in which the FSA sought engagement and views on the nature, prevalence and provision of Family Office-type services being offered by way of business, in or from the Island.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), Small States, 7.2.7 Commercially Exposed Persons - d9146f2779d154b0
body:
Recently the FSA has commenced requesting data in relation to Commercially Exposed Persons (CEPs) from firms in the Annual AML/CFT return. CEPs are individuals who are associated with a specific industry or activity which typically has a higher exposure to bribery and corruption, which, in turn, may increase the TF risk posed to the firm by such individuals where they are connected to a customer. An individual would be regarded as a CEP due to their position as a senior executive of a commercial enterprise in an industry posing a higher-risk of financial crime.
CEPs are connected to customers who are employed in or associated with the following occupational activities:

- Arms/weapons trading, dealing and defence

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), Small States, 7.2.8 Levels of Awareness of TF and Trade Expertise Among the Private and Public Sectors - 2af3defca812e522
headers: 7.2.8 Levels of Awareness of TF and Trade Expertise Among the Private and Public Sectors
body:
As per Figure 7-7, the number of TF SARs is low. FIU published a paper on Typologies: "Sanctions and Trade Based Money Laundering" in February 2023 . The document helps industry better understand the potential risks they face and how to detect suspicious behaviour. This TF NRA recommends that TF typologies are updated, including emerging threats, followed by further training to industry. It also suggests more agency training.

Therefore, there is an acknowledgement that whilst ML knowledge across the Island is good, further TF training would aid industry and the agencies, which may increase the number of TF SARs raised.

The Monaco Guidelines also look at "the extent to which there is sufficient skill base to investigate terrorism and TF and supervise compliance with TF requirements." Data is collated from the sectors, by the FSA, on number of Full Time Employees (FTE), which allows analysis to identify potential vulnerabilities within a sector on:

- Overall staff (FTE) vacancies

- Compliance staff (FTE) as a percentage of the overall staff (FTE) number

- Number of compliance staff (FTE) vacancies.

Figure 7-24 shows the staff numbers and vacancies as a percentage by each sector.

Figure 7-24: Staff Numbers and Vacancies by Sector As a Percentage

Source: FSA AML/CFT Annual Returns

headers: 7.2.9 Fintech, Regtech and Other Developing Technologies
body:
The authorities and private sector have a range of understanding of Fintech, Regtech, blockchain and other developing technologies. The FSA has a strategic goal to work with stakeholders to embrace innovation within a dynamic, appropriately regulated IFC. It is a member of the Global Financial Innovation Network (GFIN) which enables the Authority to connect with like-minded regulators and industry bodies across the globe to monitor and collaborate on Fintech developments.

A number of Government bodies support and promote developing technologies, such as DfE, IOM Digital and IOM Finance. Local firms also promote their specialist services.

The 2024 MER states:

- " Argentina assesses its TF risk as overall medium-low, especially considering the presence of transnational organisations in neighbouring jurisdictions (e.g., individuals sympathetic or related to Hezbollah, designated as a terrorist organisation by Argentina) which take advantage of the country's long and porous borders, including the TBA , to move in and out of Argentina and could use the jurisdiction to fund their activities."

In the 2024 MER, Immediate Outcome 9, TF Investigations and Prosecutions was rated as Moderate, with a number of recommended actions.

The financial flows to and from Argentina are comparatively small and 99.1% of Argentinian personal customers are within the Life Insurance sector, where the TF risk is assessed as medium low.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), Small States, 7.2.11 State Sponsorship of Terrorism - f14d0b879e6f9271
body:
This Chapter considers the issue of state sponsorship of terrorism and how this could be considered by the Island. The jurisdictions subject to a 'FATF call on its members and other jurisdictions to apply countermeasures' identifies the following countries:

- Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK)

In the Financial Flow data over the 4 years 2020/3, there were:

- DPRK - no transactions

- Iran - 19 reported inflow transactions, averaging approximately £5,000 each. No outflow transactions.

From the annual AML/CFT returns in 2023, there were:

- DPRK - no customers

- Iran.

- Iran - a very small number of personal customers across the Banking sector and Life Insurance sector and a very small number of UBOs across the Banking sector, TCSP sector and Life Insurance sector.

Whilst the exposure to the IOM from these two jurisdictions is extremely small, the risk from state-sponsored terrorism is the risk of more sophisticated financial operations servicing terrorist organisations. In a written submission in 2023 to the UK Parliament , Emily Winterbotham, Director of Terrorism and Conflict at RUSI, highlighted a number of potential risks of statesponsored terrorism, including:

- Targeting specific individuals and organisations

- Cyber-attacks

- Chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear materials related attacks

- Assassinations on UK soil

- Funding anti-democratic movements to undermine the rule of law and social cohesion

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 8. Summary & Proposed actions, 8.1 Step 5: Overall Results, TF THREAT BY TERRORIST ORGANISATION - a24d3211ef1ac19e
body:
The IOM has never experienced a domestic terrorist attack. The IOMC has a relevant intelligence gathering strategy. No terror groups or cells are believed to be active or present on the Island. There have been 4 offences between 2020 - 2023 initially recorded when reported as terrorism offences, which were hoax calls to institutions such as schools. These were later assessed to be misuse of telecommunications rather than terrorism offences.

There have been no terrorism offences and no terrorism financing offences within the scope of the time period of this NRA. The IOM population profile is low risk for terrorism. Although there are significant numbers of people resident who were not born on the Island, very few originate from regions/countries with an elevated risk profile for terrorism. There have been no terrorism prosecutions or convictions.

The overall summary of crime recorded terrorism offences for the IOMC within the time parameters of this NRA is there have been no substantive offences of terrorism, with no links to any form of fund raising from any particular example, therefore the overall domestic and cross-border TF threat is deemed very low. However, there is an assumption that the Island is not immune from the challenges faced in other countries and therefore consideration is given to the neighbours of UK and Ireland.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 8. Summary & Proposed actions, 8.1 Step 5: Overall Results, NATIONAL TF THREAT - 7a34ad8a75d0102b
body:
Figure 8-2 shows the paths of domestic and international flows of terrorist property within and between jurisdictions, adapted from The Negative Effects Of Money Laundering On Economic Development by Bartlett (May 2002). As an IFC, it is helpful to think about where the threat resides. For the Island, from the analysis, it can be summarised as:

- Domestic: There is a very low threat of domestic terrorism, therefore the threat of domestic TF is medium low

- Inbound: There is a very low threat of domestic terrorism, therefore the threat of inbound TF is medium low

- Outbound: There is the possibility of outbound TF, although this is more likely to be inadvertent and unintentional. There is also a risk that funds raised in the Island for legitimate purposes may be diverted subsequently to support foreign terrorism. The threat is medium low.

- Returning: There is a very low threat of domestic terrorism, therefore the threat of returning TF is medium low

- Flow-through: The greater risks come from the Island's crossborder business as an IFC being used to support foreign terrorism, by funds flowing through or administered from the IOM (transit). The threat is medium.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 8. Summary & Proposed actions, 8.1 Step 5: Overall Results, NATIONAL TF THREAT - f32c77d39bf78a98
body:
The Island has very close links to the UK and 38.2% of the population were born in the UK, therefore it cannot be assumed that the challenges the UK face will not be faced in the Island in the future. It is also assumed that the Island faces similar potential threats as other jurisdictions, though a smaller population will result in a proportionally smaller risk. This NRA considers that the Island could potentially face similar threats to those highlighted in the UK NRA, such as extremists (political or religious) or lone wolf actors, even though none have materialised to date.
The TF threat to the NPO sector will be considered in the NPO TF NRA which will follow the publication of this NRA. VAs will also be considered in a separate NRA. Further analysis is planned within the LPA NRA, which is scheduled for 2025. This will primarily consider the ML risks, but will also look at TF risks for LPAs.
Figure 8-2: Domestic and International Flows
Source: The Negative Effects Of Money Laundering On Economic Development by Bartlett (May 2002)
Using WB methodology and with data and the expert opinions from the Island's key agencies, government and regulators, the national threat was assessed and categorised under four TF threat categories, see Figure 8-3. As would be anticipated for an IFC, the outgoing and transit TF threat came out highest.

body:
Generally, there is a lower understanding across both agencies and industry of TF and the forms it may take compared with ML. TF may be rarely, if ever, encountered whereas ML is more common. The lack of experience in the IOM in encountering TF, a lack of experience which is shared by many jurisdictions, may mean that any warning signs of TF and the threats of and vulnerabilities to TF might not be as readily identified as they would be for ML and suspicions may not be as readily engaged and reported as they would be for ML. The very low number of TF SARs may be because there has been very little TF or potential TF to date and/or it could be partly accounted for by the lack of experience in this area.

The jurisdiction's lack of experience in dealing with TF increases the need to raise the understanding (with the assistance of experience obtained from examples encountered in other jurisdictions) of the risks, threats and vulnerabilities of TF in all agencies and across all sectors. The typologies of TF, particularly those forms of TF at risk of being encountered in an IFC, need to continue to be collected from examples encountered in other jurisdictions and disseminated so that those in a position to report suspicions of TF have a better understanding of the forms in which it may be encountered.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 8. Summary & Proposed actions, 8.1 Step 5: Overall Results, TARGETED FINANCIAL SANCTIONS - 3ed744b1eee732a9
body:
TOCFRA ensures that funds or other assets of a designated person sanctioned under a TF-related UN sanctions regime are frozen without delay and without prior notice. Under the UN sanctions regimes, there is an obligation to freeze all funds, financial assets or economic resources of designated persons. No funds or other assets have been frozen in relation to designated persons or entities under the UN TF-related TFS regimes. However, IOM regulated entities have frozen assets linked to other sanctions regimes, including the UK's Russia regime which saw an unprecedented number of individuals and entities being designated following Russia's illegal invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. This demonstrates that regulated entities understand their obligations regarding TFS.

Through examples of cooperation between agencies and actions taken in relation to other sanctions regimes, the Island can show that if there were an identified TF case, the Island would be capable of taking actions consistent with the requirements under UN sanctions regimes.

headers: MONACO (MONEYVAL) SMALL STATES GUID- ANCE ON IDENTIFYING, ASSESSING AND UNDERSTANDING THE RISK OF TF
body:
Effective measures to address TF can only be put in place if the risks are understood. This can be a challenge for smaller financial centres, such as the IOM which is an IFC.

There are several challenges:

- Extremely limited number of cases to study and competent authorities who have little experience of TF activity

- Potentially very small sums that are involved in attacks or to maintain small terrorist entities, versus the large sums required to maintain the largest terrorist entity

- The difficulty of trying to assess a risk that exists in another jurisdiction.

To help these jurisdictions, several countries met in Monaco in 2018 and 2024 (including the IOM) to provide guidance on how these smaller jurisdictions could identify, understand and assess these risks. This guidance has been used in this TF NRA in support of the WB methodology.

Consideration of the cross-border exposure for a regulated entity as well as the Island are very important to the assessment of TF. In Chapter 7.2, this TF NRA considers a number of the risks identified in the Small States Guidance.

headers: PUBLIC SECTOR AND INDUSTRY WORK TOGETHER TO ACHIEVE A COMMON GOAL OF MEETING INTERNATIONAL STANDARDS
1. Test CFT systems with hypothetical yet realistic scenarios
body:
As is the case in a number of similar jurisdictions, the exposure to terrorism and TF is extremely low and therefore it is not unusual that there are few investigations/prosecutions and convictions. Given the recent (internal only) publication of the Prosecution Policy Guidance on Terrorist Financing Prosecutions within the AGC, it is recommended that the IOM undertake an Island-wide scenario test of how the agencies and regulators would approach a real TF case. This would allow all interested parties to test that their controls work, the framework does what is intended, the handovers between agencies are efficient and terrorist financiers can be prosecuted and appropriately sanctioned and deprived of their funds/assets. The FATF Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment Guidance published in July 2019 provides suggested approaches and hypothetical scenarios. Other smaller jurisdictions have run these scenarios and their experiences and learnings will support the exercise.

To support this exercise it is recommended that more of the processes that cross several agencies are mapped to better understand the handovers and how the end-to-end process might be improved and if there are any gaps.

It is recommended that agencies conduct a 'table top' exercise to identify and address gaps in domestic information sharing pathways.

4. Targeted Financial Sanctions Familiarity and Testing
body:
It is recommended that given changes over time, it would be helpful to provide a visual picture of where responsibilities reside. Sanctions sit across a number of agencies, including: C&I, who are responsible for awareness/policy and legislation, licences and civil actions; the FIU, who receive reports of suspected breaches and frozen assets; PIMLIT; who currently have responsibility for criminal investigation of breaches; and the FSA/GSC who are responsible for supervision of the preventative measures.

The FSA and GSC's TFS supervisory approach should be strengthened and potentially have a TF lead. This person would be the contact point for TF matters and focus their learning as such on this topic. The supervisors should include applying higher scrutiny to TFS supervision, especially on-site examination checks and increasing the capability of the obliged entities to identify close associations and indirect links to sanctioned persons to better prevent sanctions evasion risks.

body:
It is recommended that consideration is given to Class 8 Money Transmission Services providing relevant financial flow data (incoming and outgoing) to the FSA on a quarterly basis.

There is no data held centrally on use of ATMs overseas. It is recommended that this data is collected (if available) from relevant businesses in the regulated sector.

EMIs are potentially importing risk to the IOM, probably from the UK. Therefore it is recommended that the banks are approached to see what financial flow data is available to analyse the risk to the Island.

One of the main TF risks that the Island faces as an IFC is use as a transit jurisdiction for the movement of funds intended to finance terrorism. Therefore, an important current activity is the analysis of incoming and outgoing financial flows to/ from high-risk countries, which increases the awareness of the relevant authorities. It is recommended that this process is documented for how this data is used by the FSA and the FIU and how regularly and how often presented with comments to appropriate governance.

As part of the strategic financial flow analysis, the FIU and FSA will consider the flows from the Island to IFCs in a similar way to the analysis with financial flows to higher-risk jurisdictions.

It is recommended that the NRAs will be reviewed every two years, to identify if there are any significantly material changes that need to be reflected in the NRA. The NRA will also be reviewed on a trigger event basis if there is a substantive local or domestic event that impacts the TF risk to the Island or if the Island Plan/National Financial Crime Strategy require an NRA to be reviewed. Via the FCSB, recommendations will be made as to which sectors to be reviewed or existing risk assessments that require to be refreshed (at least on a 5-year cycle).

An NRA will be written for VAs, which will also consider the TF risk. Should the VA TF risk materially differ from this jurisdictional TF assessment, then it will be considered as a trigger event and this NRA will also be reviewed in the light of the additional information.

body:
It is recommended that information and intelligence from all sea and air routes coming into and from the IOM be gathered in a central hub/system. This central hub will allow the sharing of information with relevant enforcement agencies to enhance the understanding of the vulnerabilities; help maximise intelligence opportunities; develop evidence-based understanding of the CTA threats; enhance collaborative working; disrupt and deter terrorist and criminal exploitation of the CTA. This will result in an improvement to the quantity and quality of the information and intelligence collected which in turn will allow for more efficient and informed investigations to be carried out by the Island's enforcement agencies.

It is recommended that Visa application information is shared by Immigration with the other competent authorities when appropriate.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 8. Summary & Proposed actions, 8.3 Updating this NRA - bedd88caf143c8d2
body:
The FATF Terrorist Financing Risk Assessment Guidance (2019) emphasises 'the importance of establishing regular mechanisms to monitor TF risks on an ongoing basis.' The National Financial Crime Strategy confirms that the Island will conduct 'a National Risk Assessment underpinned by sectoral and focussed risk assessments and addressing the risks identified on a bi-annual basis'.

The TF NRA will be reviewed every 2 years, to identify if there are any material changes that need to be reflected in the NRA. The NRA will also be reviewed on a trigger event basis if there is a substantive local or domestic event that impacts the TF risk to the Island or if the Island Plan/National Financial Crime Strategy require an NRA to be reviewed.

chunk_id: Terrorist Financing National Risk Assessment (July 2025), 8. Summary & Proposed actions, 8.4 How Industry Should Use National Risk Assessments - b1cb1d1d902ccdeb
headers: 8.4 How Industry Should Use National Risk Assessments
body:
One of the key inputs to the Island's NRAs is the risk data provided to the FSA via STRIX AML. Where published NRAs and sector reports include aggregated industry data, each firm should consider how their own data compares with the published data. This will assist them to better understand their risk profile compared to the national metrics, threats and vulnerabilities.
Businesses in the regulated sector are obliged by the Code to undertake and update the BRA, which 'assists relevant persons to understand where, when, how and to what extent they are exposed to ML/TF risk and which areas of their business they should prioritise in combatting ML/TF.' The Code states that a BRA must have regard to any relevant findings of the most recent NRA relating to the Island. Therefore, Industry must be able to show how they have considered and mitigated the relevant risks identified in this NRA. Given a number of NRAs are being published over the course of a few months, it is acceptable to consider each NRA as it is published, but update the overall BRA at its next formal review date. Consideration should also be given to the CRA and TRA and if these require updating.
In January 2024 the FSA published a thematic review of BRAs for the TCSP sector. The review considers paragraph 5(3)(b) of the Code and provides areas for consideration in a BRA.
